5. The Forms of Ownership.intro: This chapter explores the ways American law allows ownership to be divided, limiting an owner's absolute power in favor of social policy. The first unit introduces the numerus clausus: the fixed menu of estates for splitting ownership over time, from the fee simple to the life estate, and their corresponding future interests. The second unit details the rules governing these temporal divisions: the doctrine of waste, which prevents present owners from harming future interests, and the rule against restraints on alienation, which promotes marketability. The final unit shifts to concurrent ownership, examining how multiple people can own property at the same time and the rules for managing and partitioning their shared rights. Together, these doctrines show how property rights are relational and subject to limits imposed by law.

traditional_forms_of_property.summary: American law lets owners split ownership over time using only a fixed menu of estates (the numerus clausus). Each present estate that can end creates a corresponding future interest, and the specific labels of these interests determine which legal rules apply.

rules.rule: Numerus Clausus: The law recognizes only a fixed, closed list of property estates; courts will not enforce novel or customized forms of ownership.

Defeasible Fees: A fee simple can be made defeasible, ending automatically upon a stated event (determinable), giving the grantor a right to re-enter upon a condition (subject to condition subsequent), or shifting automatically to a third party (subject to executory limitation).
Future Interests: Future interests are either retained by the grantor (reversion, possibility of reverter, right of entry) or created in a third party (remainder, executory interest).

Remainders vs. Executory Interests: A remainder waits for the natural termination of the prior estate and never follows a fee simple. An executory interest divests (cuts short) a prior interest or follows a gap in possession.

Vested vs. Contingent Remainders: A remainder is vested if the taker is born and ascertained and there is no condition precedent. It is contingent if the taker is unborn/unascertained or there is a condition precedent.

Rule Against Perpetuities (RAP): Contingent remainders, executory interests, and open class gifts are void unless they must vest or fail within 21 years of the death of some life in being at the creation of the interest.

Presumption of Fee Simple: Modern statutes presume a grantor conveys their entire interest unless the instrument clearly shows a contrary intention to create a lesser estate. [[Williams v. Estate of Williams]]

cases.question: Did a will giving a farm to three daughters 'during their lives' and ending their interest if they married create a fee simple or a more limited estate?
cases.answer: The daughters received a determinable life estate, not a fee simple, because the will's language and stated purpose showed a clear 'contrary intention' to create a limited support-based interest.
cases.why: This case shows that the modern statutory presumption favoring a fee simple can be overcome by clear language in the grant expressing the grantor's intent to create a lesser estate.

tensions: Grantor Intent vs. Public Policy: Courts try to honor a grantor's intent, as in [[Williams v. Estate of Williams]], but will override it to enforce policies like the numerus clausus (prohibiting new estate types) or the Rule Against Perpetuities (promoting marketability).

Formalism vs. Function: The classification of an interest often depends on formalistic wording ('so long as' vs. 'but if') or even punctuation, which can feel arbitrary but determines crucial rights like whether forfeiture is automatic.

Presumption of Fee Simple vs. Reading the 'Four Corners': There is a tension between the modern statutory policy favoring fee simples and the judicial duty to ascertain the testator's actual intent from the entire document, as seen in the contrast between the approach in *White v. Brown* and [[Williams v. Estate of Williams]].
traps: Confusing Words of Limitation and Purchase: 'To A and her heirs' gives a fee simple to A; her heirs get nothing from the grant. 'To A for life, then to her heirs' creates a remainder in the heirs. Don't give A's heirs a present interest in the first case.

Misidentifying Future Interests: A remainder NEVER follows a fee simple. If a grant creates a fee simple that can be cut short in favor of a third party, that third party has an executory interest, not a remainder.

Applying RAP to the Wrong Interests: The Rule Against Perpetuities applies ONLY to contingent remainders, executory interests, and open class gifts. Do not apply it to vested remainders or any future interest held by the grantor (reversion, possibility of reverter, right of entry).
traditional_forms_of_property.exam_tip: Diagram every grant on a timeline: present estate first, then who takes next and when, then any condition. Name each interest, then run the Rule Against Perpetuities only on contingent remainders, executory interests and open class gifts.

waste_restraints_on_alienation.summary: When ownership is split over time, the present owner has a duty not to harm the value of the future interest (waste), and a grantor's power to restrict the sale of a fee simple is sharply limited (restraints on alienation).

rules.rule: Affirmative Waste: A present interest holder is liable for voluntary acts that permanently injure the future interest, such as destroying a valuable building. [[Brokaw v. Fairchild]]
Permissive Waste: A present interest holder is liable for failing to take reasonable care of the property, such as not paying property taxes or failing to make ordinary repairs.

Ameliorative Waste: Traditionally, a present interest holder may not make substantial changes to the property's character, even if the change increases market value, if the future interest holder objects. [[Brokaw v. Fairchild]]

Absolute Restraints on Alienation are Void: A condition that completely prohibits the owner of a fee simple from selling the property is void as against public policy. [[Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82 v. Toscano]]

Use Restrictions vs. Alienation Restraints: A condition restricting the *use* of property is generally valid and can create a defeasible fee, even if it indirectly hinders saleability. This is distinct from a direct restraint on alienation. [[Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82 v. Toscano]]
Forfeiture Restraints: A forfeiture restraint ('if A tries to sell, the land goes to B') is generally void on a fee simple but valid on a life estate.

cases.question: Can a life tenant demolish a valuable but unprofitable mansion to build a more profitable apartment building over the remaindermen's objections?
cases.answer: No; the life tenant must pass on the inheritance substantially unchanged in character, and such a demolition constitutes waste, even if it increases the property's market value.
cases.why: This case establishes the traditional, strict rule against ameliorative waste, prioritizing the remainderman's right to receive the specific thing devised over the life tenant's desire for maximum economic return.

cases.question: Is a condition in a deed that property revert to the grantor if it is sold OR if it ceases to be used for a specific purpose entirely void as a restraint on alienation?
cases.answer: No; the direct restraint on sale is void, but the restriction on use is valid and severable, creating a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.
cases.why: This case illustrates the critical, if fine, line between a void restraint on alienation and a valid use restriction that creates a defeasible fee.

tensions: Preservation vs. Economic Efficiency: Waste doctrine pits the future interest holder's right to receive the property as it was ([[Brokaw v. Fairchild]]) against the present owner's desire to put the property to its highest and best economic use, a goal modern courts increasingly favor.

Grantor Intent vs. Alienability: The law struggles to balance a grantor's desire to control property into the future with the strong public policy favoring the free transfer of land, as shown in [[Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82 v. Toscano]] where the court severs a grant to uphold part of the intent while voiding the direct restraint.

Form vs. Substance in Restraints: The dissent in [[Mountain Brow Lodge No. 82 v. Toscano]] argues that a restriction on use 'by the lodge only' is functionally identical to a restraint on alienation. The majority's focus on the formal distinction highlights a key tension in this area of law.
traps: Confusing Waste with Permissible Use: Not every change is waste. A life tenant can generally continue existing uses (like mining from an open mine) and is only liable for failing to make *reasonable* repairs, not for all depreciation.

Ignoring the Type of Estate: The rules on restraints on alienation are different for fee simples and life estates. A forfeiture restraint is usually void on a fee simple but valid on a life estate. Always identify the estate first.

Assuming All Restraints are Void: While absolute restraints on fee simples are void, reasonable restraints (e.g., rights of first refusal at market price, time-limited restrictions) may be upheld. Do not declare every restriction on sale invalid without analysis.
waste_restraints_on_alienation.exam_tip: Ask first whether a clause limits *transfer* (likely void if on a fee) or *use* (likely a valid defeasible fee), and whether it can be severed from the rest of the grant.

concurrent_owners.summary: Co-owners each own an undivided share and may possess the whole property. The form of co-ownership—tenancy in common, joint tenancy, or tenancy by the entirety—determines rights of survivorship and exposure to creditors, while partition provides the ultimate exit.

rules.rule: Three Forms of Co-ownership: Property can be held as a tenancy in common (default, no survivorship), joint tenancy (requires four unities, includes right of survivorship), or tenancy by the entirety (for married couples, with survivorship and protection from individual creditors).
Right of Survivorship: In a joint tenancy, when one co-owner dies, their interest is automatically extinguished, and the surviving co-owner(s) own the entire property. [[Harms v. Sprague]]

Severance of Joint Tenancy by Mortgage (Lien vs. Title Theory): In a 'lien theory' state, a mortgage by one joint tenant does not sever the joint tenancy because it is only a lien, not a transfer of title. [[Harms v. Sprague]] In a 'title theory' state, it does.

Ouster: A co-tenant in possession is not liable for rent to non-possessing co-tenants unless there has been an ouster—an act of excluding the other co-tenant, such as refusing a clear demand for access. [[Gillmor v. Gillmor]]
Partition: Any tenant in common or joint tenant has a right to partition. Partition in kind (physical division) is strongly preferred over partition by sale. [[Delfino v. Vealencis]]

Partition by Sale Test: A court will order a partition by sale only if (1) physical division is impracticable or inequitable, AND (2) a sale would better promote the interests of *all* owners. [[Delfino v. Vealencis]]

Professional Degrees in Divorce: While most states do not treat a professional degree as marital property, a supporting spouse may have an equitable claim for their financial and other contributions toward its attainment. [[Postema v. Postema]]

cases.question: Should a court order a partition by sale, sought by a developer co-owner, over a partition in kind, sought by a co-owner who lives and runs a business on the property?
cases.answer: No; partition in kind is strongly preferred, and a sale should only be ordered if physical division is impracticable and a sale better serves the interests of *all* owners, not just the economic interest of one.
cases.why: This case establishes the strong judicial preference for partition in kind and protects the non-economic, possessory interests of a co-tenant against the purely financial interests of another.

cases.question: Is a co-tenant who uses the entire property liable to another co-tenant if the other co-tenant demands to use the land and is refused?
cases.answer: Yes; refusing a co-tenant's clear demand for use constitutes an ouster, making the occupying tenant liable for the rental value of the excluded tenant's share.
cases.why: This case clarifies what constitutes an 'ouster,' moving beyond physical exclusion to include situations where one co-tenant's use to full capacity and refusal to accommodate another effectively bars access.

cases.question: In a 'lien theory' state, does a mortgage by one joint tenant sever the joint tenancy, and does the mortgage survive his death?
cases.answer: No; a mortgage is merely a lien and does not destroy any of the four unities, so it does not sever the joint tenancy, and the lien is extinguished when the mortgagor's interest vanishes at death.
cases.why: This case shows the critical importance of a state's theory of mortgages (lien vs. title) in determining the rights of joint tenants and their creditors.

cases.question: Can a spouse who supported their partner through professional school receive compensation for their contributions upon divorce, even if the degree itself isn't 'property'?
cases.answer: Yes; the supporting spouse has an equitable claim for compensation for their contributions and sacrifices made as part of a 'concerted family effort' to obtain the degree.
cases.why: This case expands the concept of marital assets to include equitable claims based on contributions to non-traditional assets like professional degrees, focusing on fairness rather than strict property definitions.

tensions: Freedom of Exit vs. Protecting Reliance Interests: Any co-tenant has an absolute right to partition, but this right clashes with the reliance interests of a co-tenant in possession, as seen in [[Delfino v. Vealencis]], where the court protects a resident's home and business over a developer's desire for a profitable sale.

Formalism vs. Creditor Rights: The outcome in [[Harms v. Sprague]] results from a formalistic application of joint tenancy's survivorship feature and the lien theory of mortgages, prioritizing the form of ownership over a creditor's seemingly valid claim.

Property as a Thing vs. Property as a Right: The marital property cases ([[Postema v. Postema]]) struggle with whether a professional degree is 'property.' The court sidesteps the definition by creating an 'equitable claim,' showing a tension between treating property as a tangible thing and as a bundle of rights deserving equitable protection.
traps: Forgetting the Four Unities: To create a joint tenancy, the unities of time, title, interest, and possession must be present. If a grant gives A a 1/3 share and B a 2/3 share, it cannot be a joint tenancy because the unity of interest is missing; it is a tenancy in common.

Assuming a Mortgage Always Severs: Severance by mortgage depends on whether the state follows the lien theory (no severance, per [[Harms v. Sprague]]) or title theory (severance). On an exam, if the jurisdiction isn't specified, analyze the outcome under both theories.

Miscalculating Rights to Rent: A co-tenant in possession owes no rent to others *unless* there is an ouster, an agreement to pay rent, or they are collecting rent from a third party. Don't automatically make the occupying tenant pay.
concurrent_owners.exam_tip: Identify the form of co-ownership first (survivorship?). Then check for severance (e.g., a conveyance, or a mortgage in a title-theory state). Then analyze rights between the owners (ouster, accounting). Finally, consider the exit strategy (partition).

1. What is Property?.intro: This chapter introduces the foundational question of property law: what is it and why does the law protect it? We begin with the owner’s core right to exclude, exploring its fierce protection in trespass law ([[Jacque v. Steenberg Homes]]) and its limits in the face of new technologies ([[Hinman v. Pacific Air Transport]]). Next, we examine nuisance, the doctrine governing conflicts between neighboring land uses, where courts balance competing interests to determine when one owner’s use unreasonably interferes with another’s enjoyment ([[Hendricks v. Stalnaker]]). Finally, we explore how property rights are first acquired in unowned things through first possession and capture ([[Pierson v. Post]]), and how this principle interacts with the rights of existing landowners. Together, these units frame the course’s central tension: when does the law grant absolute protection to owners, and what principles—like public interest, reasonableness, or prior possession—can trump an owner’s claim?

trespass_introductory_concepts.summary: Trespass protects the owner's fundamental right to exclusive possession of their land. An intentional physical invasion is a trespass, even if it causes no actual harm, but this absolute right has limits, especially in the airspace far above the ground.

rules.rule: The private landowner's right to exclude others from their land is one of the most essential rights of property.
In Wisconsin, when nominal damages are awarded for an intentional trespass to land, punitive damages may be awarded to deter misconduct and vindicate the right to exclude.
In an intentional trespass to land, actual harm occurs in the violation of the legal right to exclude, even if that harm is not measurable in dollars.

The ad coelum doctrine ('to the heavens and to the depths') is rejected as a literal rule; a landowner owns only as much of the space above the ground as they can occupy or make use of in connection with the enjoyment of their land.
Use of airspace by others that is injurious to the land or constitutes an actual interference with the owner's possession or beneficial use is a trespass; mere flight through unused airspace is not.

cases.question: Can a landowner sue for trespass when airplanes fly high above their unused land, without causing any actual damage or interference?
cases.answer: Appellees (airlines) won; a landowner's property rights in airspace are limited to the portion they can actually use, and mere flight through unused airspace without actual damage is not a trespass.
cases.why: This case establishes that the right to exclude is not infinite, limiting the traditional 'ad coelum' doctrine to create a public right of transit in the upper airspace.

cases.question: Can a jury award large punitive damages for an intentional trespass that caused only $1 in nominal damages?
cases.answer: Plaintiff (Jacques) won; the court held that for intentional trespass to land, punitive damages can be awarded even with only nominal damages to protect the fundamental right to exclude.
cases.why: This case strongly affirms the right to exclude as a central pillar of property, justifying significant punishment to deter intentional violations, even when no economic harm occurs.

tensions: Absolute vs. Limited Rights: The right to exclude is nearly absolute on the ground ([[Jacque v. Steenberg Homes]]), but is limited to actual use in the sky ([[Hinman v. Pacific Air Transport]]). This creates a tension about where one zone ends and the other begins.

Property Rules vs. Efficiency: [[Jacque v. Steenberg Homes]] protects the landowner's right to be 'irrational' and refuse a trespass, even if the trespass would be economically efficient. This prioritizes owner sovereignty over social utility.

Harm vs. Right: Does a trespass cause harm because it damages the property, or is the violation of the right to exclude itself the harm? [[Jacque v. Steenberg Homes]] argues the latter, justifying damages even without physical injury.
traps: Applying 'ad coelum' literally. Do not state that a landowner owns 'to the heavens.' [[Hinman v. Pacific Air Transport]] explicitly rejects this. Ownership is limited by a standard of reasonableness and actual or potential use.

Confusing trespass with nuisance. Trespass protects exclusive possession against physical entry; nuisance protects use and enjoyment. Under [[Hinman v. Pacific Air Transport]], flights through airspace the owner isn't using or likely to use are not a trespass; flights low and frequent enough to interfere with actual use can be (and, by the government, can be a taking: *United States v. Causby*). Noise and vibration from flights are usually analyzed as nuisance.

Assuming the [[Jacque v. Steenberg Homes]] punitive damages rule is universal. The court in *Jacque* created an exception to the general rule that punitive damages require compensatory damages. Note that this is a Wisconsin rule and may not apply in other jurisdictions.

Ignoring intent. The holding in [[Jacque v. Steenberg Homes]] is about *intentional* trespass. An accidental or negligent trespass would likely be treated differently, with damages limited to actual harm caused.
trespass_introductory_concepts.exam_tip: On an exam, if you see a physical invasion of land, start with a trespass analysis. Ask: Was the invasion intentional? Did it cross the boundary? If so, it's a trespass, and at least nominal damages are available. If the invasion is in the air, apply [[Hinman v. Pacific Air Transport]]: is it interfering with the owner's actual or potential use of the land? If not, it's likely not a trespass.

nuisance.summary: Nuisance law governs conflicts between landowners, protecting the right to the use and enjoyment of land from substantial and unreasonable interference. Unlike trespass, nuisance almost always involves a balancing of competing interests to determine if a defendant's conduct is 'unreasonable.'

rules.rule: A private nuisance is a substantial and unreasonable interference with the private use and enjoyment of another’s land.
An intentional interference is unreasonable if the gravity of the harm outweighs the social value of the activity alleged to cause the harm.

In Michigan, recovery for trespass requires a direct or immediate intrusion of a physical, tangible object; intangible invasions like dust, noise, and vibrations are properly addressed under nuisance law.

In a suit for *damages* for nuisance in Wisconsin, the court does not balance the utility of the defendant's conduct against the gravity of the injury; due care is not a defense if substantial injury occurs.
A lawful business can be enjoined as a nuisance when it causes substantial injury to a neighbor's property that damages cannot adequately remedy; whether a use is reasonable depends on its locality.

Where a developer brings a residential population to a lawful, pre-existing agricultural or industrial operation, thereby creating a public nuisance, the operation may be enjoined, but the developer may be required to indemnify the operator for the costs of moving or shutting down.
cases: [[Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.]]

cases.question: Can a landowner get an injunction to stop a neighboring brick-yard from emitting fumes that kill his ornamental trees, even if the brick-yard was there first?
cases.answer: The neighbors won an injunction: burning bricks with anthracite coal killed their ornamental trees, the harm was substantial and recurring, and damages were inadequate, so the lawful brickyard was a nuisance in that location.
cases.why: This is a classic case establishing that even a lawful and useful business cannot inflict substantial harm on its neighbors, justifying an injunction (a property rule) to protect the neighbor's right to enjoyment.

cases.question: In a nuisance lawsuit for money damages, can a power plant defend itself by arguing it used due care and its social utility outweighs the harm to neighboring farms?
cases.answer: Plaintiff (farmers) won; in Wisconsin, for a damages claim, neither due care nor a balancing of social utility is a defense to liability for a nuisance that causes substantial harm.
cases.why: This case establishes a minority, rights-based view of nuisance (for damages), holding that a useful enterprise cannot injure private property without paying for it, regardless of its social value or carefulness.

cases.case: [[Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.]]
cases.question: Can a cattle feedlot be shut down as a nuisance when a new retirement community is built next to it, and if so, who should pay for the shutdown?
cases.answer: Both parties won in part; the feedlot was a public nuisance and could be enjoined, but the developer who 'came to the nuisance' had to pay the feedlot's costs of moving.
cases.why: This case creates a novel 'purchased injunction' remedy, balancing the public interest in eliminating the nuisance with the fairness to a lawful business that was harmed by encroaching development.

cases.question: Is a water well a private nuisance if it prevents a neighbor from installing a septic system, when both uses are necessary and neither party has a good alternative?
cases.answer: Defendant (Stalnaker) won; the court found the well was not an unreasonable use of land because, when balancing the conflicting interests, the harm did not outweigh the utility of the well.
cases.why: This case is a perfect illustration of the balancing test at the heart of modern nuisance law, showing that when two reasonable and necessary uses conflict, the law may decline to label either one a nuisance.

cases.question: Can landowners sue for trespass due to intrusions of dust, noise, and vibrations from a nearby mine?
cases.answer: Defendant (mine) won; the court held that in Michigan, intangible invasions like dust, noise, and vibrations are not trespasses and must be brought as nuisance claims, which require proof of substantial harm.
cases.why: This case strictly separates trespass and nuisance, requiring a 'tangible' physical invasion for trespass to protect the distinct legal interests each tort covers (possession vs. use and enjoyment).

tensions: Rights vs. Balancing: Should nuisance law protect a right to be free from harm (as in [[Jost v. Dairyland Power Cooperative]] for damages), or should it balance competing interests to find the most efficient outcome (as in [[Hendricks v. Stalnaker]])?

Property Rules vs. Liability Rules: Should a court enjoin the nuisance (property rule, [[Campbell v. Seaman]]), force the polluter to pay damages but continue operating (liability rule, like *Boomer*), or make the victim pay the polluter to stop (purchased injunction, [[Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.]])?

Coming to the Nuisance: Is it fair to let a newcomer shut down a pre-existing, lawful business? [[Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.]] says yes for the public good, but no without compensation, showing the doctrine is a flexible factor, not an absolute bar.
traps: Applying the [[Jost v. Dairyland Power Cooperative]] 'no balancing' rule outside of a Wisconsin damages claim. The majority rule, seen in [[Hendricks v. Stalnaker]], is to balance the interests to determine if the interference is 'unreasonable.'

Forgetting the remedy. Don't just conclude 'it's a nuisance.' The key question is what happens next. An injunction is possible ([[Campbell v. Seaman]]), but courts may award damages or even a purchased injunction ([[Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.]]) if shutting down the defendant seems inequitable.

Misidentifying the tort. If the invasion is intangible (noise, odor, light), it's a nuisance problem, not trespass, in many jurisdictions ([[Adams v. Cleveland-Cliffs Iron Co.]]). This is critical because nuisance requires proving substantial and unreasonable harm, while intentional trespass does not.
nuisance.exam_tip: When you spot a conflict between neighboring land uses, use the nuisance framework. First, is the interference 'substantial'? Second, is it 'unreasonable'? To determine unreasonableness, balance the gravity of the harm to the plaintiff against the utility of the defendant's conduct ([[Hendricks v. Stalnaker]]). Finally, analyze the appropriate remedy: injunction, damages, or a purchased injunction as in [[Spur Industries Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co.]].

privilege_first_possession.summary: This unit explores how property rights are first established. For unowned resources like wild animals, the 'rule of capture' awards ownership to the first person to take possession, but this rule is limited by the rights of landowners and the nature of the resource itself.

rules.rule: Property in wild animals (ferae naturae) is acquired by occupancy, which requires actual corporal possession or mortally wounding the animal to bring it within the pursuer's certain control.
Mere pursuit of a wild animal does not create a property right.
Things that become naturally embedded in the soil are part of the realty and belong to the landowner, not the finder, under the principle of accession ('quicquid plantatur solo, solo cedit').
Equity will grant an injunction to prevent repeated trespasses that interfere with the peaceful enjoyment of property, especially when legal remedies (damages) are inadequate.
An owner of land can obtain an injunction to prevent the cutting of standing timber, as it is part of the realty and its destruction is an injury for which money damages are an inadequate remedy.
To obtain an injunction against timber trespass, it is not necessary to allege the trespasser's insolvency.

cases.question: Does a hunter who is merely pursuing a fox gain a property right in it, or does the right belong to the person who actually kills and captures it?
cases.answer: Pierson (the captor) won; the court established that property in wild animals is acquired by capture (taking possession), not by mere pursuit.
cases.why: This is the foundational case for the 'rule of capture,' providing a clear, bright-line rule for establishing ownership over unowned resources to promote certainty and avoid disputes.

cases.question: Who owns a meteorite that falls from the sky and embeds itself in the ground: the person who finds and digs it up, or the owner of the land?
cases.answer: Plaintiff (Goddard, the landowner) won; the meteorite became part of the soil through natural forces and thus belonged to the owner of the land.
cases.why: This case shows the limits of the 'finders keepers' rule. When an object becomes affixed to the land (accession), it belongs to the landowner, not the first person to possess it.

cases.question: Can a landowner get an injunction to stop someone from cutting timber on their land without proving the trespasser is insolvent?
cases.answer: Plaintiffs (landowners) won; the court held that cutting timber is an injury to the land itself for which damages are inadequate, so an injunction is available regardless of the trespasser's solvency.
cases.why: This case expands the availability of injunctive relief for trespass, recognizing that some property (like standing timber) has unique value that money cannot replace, thus justifying a property rule protection.

cases.question: Can a landowner get an injunction to stop a fox-hunting club from repeatedly trespassing on their farm with a pack of hounds?
cases.answer: The Bakers (landowners) won; the court held that equity can enjoin a series of trespasses that interfere with the peaceful enjoyment of property, as multiple lawsuits for small damages would be an inadequate remedy.
cases.why: This case affirms that the right to exclude can be protected by an injunction against repeated invasions, prioritizing the landowner's right to peaceful enjoyment over a trespasser's recreational custom.

tensions: First Possession vs. Landowner Sovereignty: The rule of capture from [[Pierson v. Post]] rewards the first possessor, but [[Goddard v. Winchell]] shows that this rule yields to the landowner's rights when the object in question becomes part of the land itself.

Clear Rules vs. Fairness/Policy: The majority in [[Pierson v. Post]] favored a clear, easy-to-administer rule (actual capture) to prevent disputes, while the dissent argued for a rule that would better encourage the policy goal of killing foxes.

Damages vs. Injunctions: When is money not enough? Both [[Pardee v. Camden Lumber Co.]] and [[Baker v. Howard County Hunt]] move away from a pure damages remedy for trespass, granting injunctions to protect the owner's non-economic interests in their land (keeping it in its natural state, peaceful enjoyment).
traps: Misapplying the rule of capture. The rule from [[Pierson v. Post]] is for unowned, wild things (res nullius). It does not apply to things that are already part of someone's land ([[Goddard v. Winchell]]) or to domesticated animals.

Assuming an injunction requires irreparable harm in the sense of insolvency. [[Pardee v. Camden Lumber Co.]] explicitly rejects this for timber trespass, redefining the inadequacy of legal remedy to include the unique nature of the property itself.

Ignoring the context of the 'capture.' While [[Pierson v. Post]] was on 'waste land,' a trespasser who captures an animal on private land may still lose title to the landowner. The right to hunt does not include the right to trespass ([[Baker v. Howard County Hunt]]).
privilege_first_possession.exam_tip: When you see a conflict over an object, first ask: is this thing owned or unowned? If unowned (like a wild fox), apply the rule of capture from [[Pierson v. Post]]. If it's attached to or part of someone's land (like a meteorite or timber), the landowner owns it ([[Goddard v. Winchell]], [[Pardee v. Camden Lumber Co.]]). If the issue is repeated entry onto land, even if minor, consider an injunction to prevent a multiplicity of suits ([[Baker v. Howard County Hunt]]).

2. Acquisition and Claim Scope.intro: This chapter explores how property rights are first acquired and defined. It moves from foundational, sovereign-level claims based on 'discovery' to individual acquisition through creation, finding lost items, and adding value through labor (accession). The chapter culminates in adverse possession, a doctrine where a long-term possessor can wrest title from the 'true' owner. These units collectively address the course's central question by examining the various acts—from discovery and creation to simple, sustained possession—that the law recognizes as sufficient to create ownership. They also reveal what can defeat a seemingly valid ownership claim, demonstrating that property rights are not absolute but are shaped by principles of labor, notice, reliance, and the efficient use of resources.

discovery_creation.summary: This unit examines how property rights are established in previously unowned things, from the sovereign's claim to a continent to a business's claim to valuable, time-sensitive information.

rules.rule: Discovery Doctrine: The European nation that 'discovers' land in the Americas gains title against all other European governments, and with it the exclusive right to extinguish the Native American 'right of occupancy' by purchase or conquest.
Private individuals cannot acquire valid title to land by purchasing it directly from Native American tribes; only the sovereign (the U.S. government) can extinguish the native title.

Quasi-Property Right: As between competitors, news gathered through labor and expense is treated as 'quasi-property,' and its systematic appropriation by a rival for commercial gain constitutes unfair competition.
Misappropriation: A business may not 'reap where it has not sown' by taking the fruits of a competitor's labor and investment for its own commercial benefit without compensation.
Publication of news to the public for its intended purpose (reading) does not constitute abandonment of the news's commercial value to a competitor.

cases.question: Can a land title purchased directly from a Native American tribe hold up in U.S. court against a later title granted by the U.S. government for the same land?
cases.answer: No, the U.S. government's title is superior because the 'discovery doctrine' gave the sovereign the exclusive right to acquire land from the native occupants.
cases.why: This case establishes the foundation of U.S. property law, subordinating first possession by native inhabitants to the rights of the conquering sovereign, thereby defining the origin of all land titles.

cases.question: Is it legal for a news agency to take breaking news from a competitor's public bulletins and early editions and sell it as its own?
cases.answer: No, INS loses because while news is not property against the public, it is 'quasi-property' between competitors, and systematically taking it is unfair competition.
cases.why: It creates the tort of misappropriation, protecting investment in intangible, information-based assets that fall outside traditional copyright or patent law.

tensions: First Possession vs. Sovereign Power: [[Johnson v. M'Intosh]] rejects a pure 'first in time' rule for Native Americans in favor of a rule based on sovereign conquest and the 'necessity' of a stable system of title derived from the U.S. government.

Protecting Investment vs. Free Competition: The majority in [[International News Service v. Associated Press]] protects AP's labor and investment, while the dissent argues that allowing appropriation of uncopyrightable facts promotes competition and the free flow of information.

Judicial Role in Creating Property: The court in [[International News Service v. Associated Press]] created a new, limited property right ('quasi-property'), while the dissent argued that such a significant policy decision should be left to the legislature.
traps: Misapplying [[International News Service v. Associated Press]] to the general public. The 'quasi-property' right in news exists only between competitors; once published, the public is free to use the information.

Oversimplifying [[Johnson v. M'Intosh]] as a 'first possession' case. The court explicitly denies the full property rights of the first possessors (the tribes) in favor of the sovereign's exclusive right to acquire title from them.

Confusing the property right in a news story (copyrightable expression) with the property right in the news itself (the facts). [[International News Service v. Associated Press]] deals with the latter, which is not copyrightable.
discovery_creation.exam_tip: When you see a fact pattern involving valuable information or data that isn't protected by copyright or patent, analyze it under [[International News Service v. Associated Press]]. Ask if one party is 'reaping where it has not sown' by appropriating the fruits of a competitor's labor and expense.

prior_possession_finders.summary: This unit establishes the principle of 'relative title,' where a finder or prior possessor of a chattel has a superior right to it against everyone in the world except the true owner or a prior possessor.

rules.rule: A finder of a lost chattel acquires a 'special property' right in it that is superior to that of any subsequent finder.
The loss of a chattel does not divest the finder of their special property right, which they can assert against a subsequent finder.

Expending labor to gather and improve the value of abandoned property (e.g., raking manure into piles) creates a property right against a subsequent taker, protected for a reasonable time to allow for removal.
Possession of property, even if wrongfully obtained, is sufficient title to maintain an action (like replevin) against a subsequent taker who is a 'mere stranger' to the property.
A defendant cannot defeat a prior possessor's claim by showing title in a third party (jus tertii defense) unless the defendant can connect themselves to that third party's title.

cases.question: If a person finds logs, moors them, and then they float away and are found by someone else, who has the better claim?
cases.answer: The first finder (Clark) wins because a finder acquires a special property right that is not lost if the item is subsequently lost and found by another.
cases.why: This case establishes the rule of 'prior possessor wins,' creating a hierarchy of rights among finders to promote order and protect possession.

cases.question: Does someone who rakes abandoned manure into piles on a public street gain a property right to it against someone who takes it the next day?
cases.answer: Yes, Haslem wins because his labor in gathering the manure gave him a property right, valid for a reasonable time, against a subsequent taker.
cases.why: It shows that labor can be a basis for establishing possession and a property right, even if that possession is temporary and not continuous.

cases.question: Can a person who wrongfully cut logs from a third party's land sue another person who takes those logs from them?
cases.answer: Yes, the first wrongful possessor (Anderson) wins because even wrongful possession is a better title than no title at all, which is what the second taker had.
cases.why: This case strongly affirms the principle of relative title, holding that possession is a powerful right against all but those with a superior claim, in order to prevent a chaotic series of seizures.

tensions: Protecting Possession vs. True Ownership: The law protects a prior possessor, even a wrongful one as in [[Anderson v. Gouldberg]], not because they are 'right,' but to discourage a 'free-for-all' where people could take property from anyone who isn't the true owner.

Labor vs. Possession: In [[Haslem v. Lockwood]], the act of raking the manure into piles was enough to constitute possession, showing that labor which adds value can be the act that establishes a property right.
traps: Assuming the finder gets absolute ownership. A finder's right is 'good against all the world *except the true owner*.' The true owner always has the superior claim.

Forgetting the rule of relative title. In a dispute between two finders, the first finder wins ([[Clark v. Maloney]]). In a dispute between two wrongful possessors, the prior possessor wins ([[Anderson v. Gouldberg]]).
prior_possession_finders.exam_tip: When you see a sequence of events where property is found, lost, and found again, or taken from a possessor, draw out the chain of possession. The key question is always: 'Between the two parties in this lawsuit, who has the superior claim?' The answer is almost always the prior possessor.

accession.summary: Accession governs disputes where one person's property is changed or added to by another's labor or materials, or by natural forces, determining who owns the resulting product.

rules.rule: Accession by Good-Faith Improver: When a person, in good faith, takes another's chattel and transforms it into a new article of substantially greater value, title passes to the improver, who is liable only for the value of the original materials.
Accession by Willful Trespasser: A willful trespasser who improves a chattel does not gain title, regardless of the degree of transformation or value added.

Accretion vs. Avulsion: Gradual and imperceptible changes to a riverbank (accretion) shift the property boundary with the river, while a sudden, violent change in the river's course (avulsion) leaves the boundary in the center of the old channel.

Fixture Test: An item of personal property becomes a fixture (part of the real estate) based on (1) actual annexation, (2) application to the use of the realty, and (3) the objective intention of the party making the annexation to make it permanent.

Fixture Intent: The intent of an owner who annexes an item is presumed to be to enrich the property and is judged objectively by the circumstances, not by their secret, uncommunicated subjective intent.
Ad Coelum Doctrine: The owner of the surface of land owns to the sky above and to the center of the earth below, but a court may order a temporary invasion (like a survey) to administer justice.

cases.question: If someone mistakenly takes timber and transforms it into barrel hoops worth 28 times more, can the original owner reclaim the hoops?
cases.answer: No, Wetherbee (the improver) wins because he acted in good faith and dramatically increased the property's value, so title transfers to him and he only owes damages for the original timber.
cases.why: This case establishes the good-faith improver rule for accession, balancing the original owner's rights against the value added by labor to avoid a punitive result.

cases.question: When a river forming a state boundary suddenly cuts a new channel, does the boundary line move with the new channel?
cases.answer: The law of accretion governs the Missouri River despite its rapid changes, so gradual shifts move the boundary; but the river's sudden 1877 cutoff was an avulsion, so for the disputed land the boundary stayed in the center of the old channel.
cases.why: It provides a clear, predictable rule for changes in boundaries caused by water, distinguishing between gradual changes (accretion) and sudden ones (avulsion).

cases.question: Can a court force a cave owner to allow a survey to see if the cave runs under a neighbor's land?
cases.answer: Yes, the judge (Sims) wins because courts have the power to order such an inspection to determine the truth, based on the 'ad coelum' doctrine that the neighbor owns the land beneath his surface.
cases.why: This case affirms the traditional 'ad coelum' doctrine for subterranean rights while also showing that a court's equitable power can justify a limited trespass to resolve a dispute.

cases.question: Can a home seller remove items like custom light fixtures and wall-mounted mirrors after the sale, claiming they are personal property?
cases.answer: No, the buyer (Strain) wins because the items were fixtures; the seller's objective intent, inferred from the circumstances, made them part of the house.
cases.why: It clarifies the modern fixture test, emphasizing that a seller's secret intent is irrelevant and that a buyer can reasonably expect attached, functional items to be included in the sale.

tensions: Protecting Title vs. Rewarding Labor: [[Wetherbee v. Green]] balances the original owner's property right against the immense value added by a good-faith improver, choosing to reward labor to avoid a disproportionate penalty.

Formal Doctrine vs. Practical Justice: The dissent in [[Edwards v. Sims]] argues against the rigid 'ad coelum' rule, proposing that the person who discovers and makes a cave valuable through labor should own it, regardless of surface lines.

Subjective Intent vs. Objective Expectations: [[Strain v. Green]] prioritizes the buyer's reasonable, objective expectations over the seller's secret subjective intent to protect the integrity of real estate transactions.
traps: Applying the [[Wetherbee v. Green]] accession rule to a bad-faith improver. A willful trespasser who transforms property never gains title and may be liable for the improved value.
Confusing accretion and avulsion in a water boundary problem. Accretion is slow and moves the boundary; avulsion is sudden and does not.
Relying on a party's testimony about their 'intent' for a fixture. [[Strain v. Green]] shows that intent is inferred objectively from the nature of the item, its use, and the mode of attachment.
accession.exam_tip: When property is altered, ask 'Who did the altering and why?' If it's a good-faith improver adding substantial value, think [[Wetherbee v. Green]]. If it's personal property attached to a house being sold, apply the three-part fixture test from [[Strain v. Green]]. If it's a river changing course, distinguish accretion from avulsion.

adverse_possession.summary: Adverse possession allows a non-owner to acquire title by possessing property for a statutory period in a manner that is actual, open, continuous, exclusive, and hostile to the true owner's rights.

rules.rule: To establish adverse possession, a claimant must prove their possession was: (1) actual, (2) open and notorious, (3) exclusive, (4) continuous for the statutory period, and (5) hostile under a claim of right.
Continuity: The nature of possession required depends on the type of property; seasonal use of a summer home is 'continuous' for adverse possession purposes.

Tacking: An adverse possessor may 'tack' their period of possession onto that of their predecessors to meet the statutory requirement, provided there is 'privity' between them (a reasonable connection, such as a sale).
Privity for Tacking: Privity can exist even if a deed mistakenly describes an adjacent parcel, as long as the parties intended to transfer, and did transfer, possession of the disputed land.

Claim of Right (Good Faith): In some jurisdictions (like Iowa), a claim of right must be in good faith. A possessor who knows they have no title and no basis for a claim cannot establish adverse possession.

Actual Possession (Wild Lands): For wild and undeveloped land, 'actual' possession can be established by acts like marking boundaries, managing timber, and leasing hunting rights, rather than constant occupation or cultivation.

Adverse Possession of Chattels: The statute of limitations for conversion of personal property can begin to run when the possessor openly and notoriously treats the property as their own (e.g., by commercial exploitation), not necessarily upon a demand and refusal.

cases.question: Can a series of owners who mistakenly occupied the wrong summer home add their periods of possession together to claim adverse possession?
cases.answer: Yes, the Kuntos win because summer-only use is 'continuous' for a summer home, and the successive owners can 'tack' their possession periods together because they were connected by privity through the sale.
cases.why: This case shows the flexibility of the 'continuity' and 'privity' elements, adapting them to the nature of the property and the reasonable expectations of good-faith purchasers.

cases.question: Can someone claim adverse possession of land they used as part of their yard if they always knew it belonged to their neighbor?
cases.answer: No, the record owner wins because the possessor (Carpenter) did not have a good-faith 'claim of right'; she knew she had no title and was essentially a squatter.
cases.why: This case represents the minority 'good faith' view of the hostility element, requiring that the adverse possessor have a genuine, albeit mistaken, belief that they own the land.

cases.question: When does the clock start running on a claim to recover master tapes that were initially possessed with permission but later commercially exploited without it?
cases.answer: The Estate wins because the claim is time-barred; the statute of limitations for conversion began when the Estate openly acted as owner by licensing the tapes, not when a formal demand for return was made.
cases.why: It illustrates how the statute of limitations for chattels (a concept analogous to adverse possession) can be triggered by an overt act of ownership, distinguishing it from the 'demand and refusal' rule used in other contexts.

cases.question: Can a company adversely possess 20 acres of wild timberland by painting a boundary line, managing the timber, and issuing hunting licenses?
cases.answer: Yes, Anderson-Tully wins because for wild and unimproved land, these public acts of ownership are sufficient to satisfy the elements of adverse possession over the 10-year statutory period.
cases.why: This case demonstrates how the standard for 'actual' and 'open' possession is adapted to the character of the land in question.

tensions: Rewarding Use vs. Protecting Title: Adverse possession's core tension is between penalizing a 'sleeping' owner and rewarding a productive user, aiming to clear stale claims and align legal title with long-standing possession.

The Meaning of 'Hostility': Jurisdictions split on the required state of mind. A good-faith standard (Iowa in [[Carpenter v. Ruperto]]) requires an honest mistaken belief of ownership; the majority objective standard asks only whether the possession was without the owner's permission; a few courts once required knowing (aggressive) trespass.

Adverse Possession of Real vs. Personal Property: While the underlying theory is similar, the rules differ. For chattels, the 'open and notorious' element is harder to meet, leading to different rules for when the statute of limitations begins to run, as seen in [[Songbyrd Inc. v. Estate of Grossman]].
traps: Forgetting to check every element. A claimant must prove all elements (Actual, Continuous, Exclusive, Open & Notorious, Hostile) for the entire statutory period. Failure on any one element is fatal to the claim.

Applying a uniform standard of 'possession' to all types of land. The requirements for 'actual' and 'continuous' use are much higher for a residence or farm than for a summer home ([[Howard v. Kunto]]) or wild timberland ([[Scott v. Anderson-Tully Co.]]).

Ignoring the possessor's state of mind. While many states use an objective test for hostility, some (like in [[Carpenter v. Ruperto]]) require good faith. Spotting facts about what the possessor knew is critical.

Miscalculating the time period. Remember to check for 'tacking' ([[Howard v. Kunto]]) and any facts that might 'toll' (pause) the statute of limitations, such as the owner's disability (infancy, insanity, etc.).
adverse_possession.exam_tip: When you see a long-term user of land who isn't the owner, immediately run through the adverse possession checklist (A.C.E.O.H.). Create a timeline to track the statutory period, noting when possession began, if it was interrupted, and if tacking applies. Pay special attention to the character of the land and the possessor's state of mind.

3. Values Subject to Ownership.intro: This chapter challenges the simple idea of property as absolute ownership over a thing. It asks: what are the outer limits of what can be owned? The first unit, 'Persons & Commodities,' explores the controversial line between person and property, examining whether human bodies and their component parts can be bought and sold. The second unit, 'Communities, Customs, Public Rights, Water,' shifts focus to how collective interests can limit or even create property rights. It shows how community custom, the public trust over navigable waters, and statutory protections for cultural heritage can trump an individual owner’s claim. Together, these units reveal that property is a complex social construct, where the law often sides with public values and community norms over the individual owner, directly addressing the course's central question.

persons_commodities.summary: This unit examines the controversial question of when human bodies and their parts can be treated as property. It explores the tension between individual autonomy, the public interest in research and health, and moral objections to commodification.

rules.rule: A patient does not retain a sufficient ownership interest in their excised cells to support a cause of action for conversion against researchers who commercialize them.
cases: [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]]

rules.rule: A physician has a fiduciary duty to disclose all personal interests, including research and economic interests, that may be material to a patient's decision to consent to medical treatment.
cases: [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]]

rules.rule: A decedent's interest in their cryogenically preserved gametes constitutes 'property' within the meaning of the probate code, to the extent that they had decision-making authority over their use for reproduction.
The National Organ Transplant Act (NOTA) prohibits giving valuable consideration for human organs, including 'bone marrow' extracted via aspiration.

NOTA's prohibition on compensating 'bone marrow' donors does not apply to hematopoietic stem cells extracted from peripheral blood via apheresis, as these are considered 'blood,' which is exempt from the statute.

Human biological materials may be treated as a unique, 'sui generis' category of property, not subject to all general property rules but still affording the 'owner' certain rights, like decisional authority over their use.
cases: [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]]

cases.case: [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]]
cases.question: Can a patient sue for conversion (theft) of his own cells after they were removed from his body and used to create a valuable patented cell line without his consent?
cases.answer: No, the court held that Moore did not retain an ownership interest in his excised cells sufficient for a conversion claim, but he could sue for breach of fiduciary duty and lack of informed consent.
cases.why: This case shows the law's deep reluctance to treat body parts as simple property, balancing a patient's right to make informed decisions against the public interest in protecting medical research from extensive liability.

cases.question: Can a court order the destruction of a deceased man's frozen sperm when his will explicitly left it to his girlfriend for the purpose of having his child?
cases.answer: No, the court found that the decedent's decision-making authority over his sperm was a property interest protected under probate law, and no public policy barred posthumous conception.
cases.why: This case establishes that gametes intended for reproduction are a form of property, unlike the cells in [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]], because of their unique potential for creating life and the donor's fundamental interest in procreation.

cases.question: Does the federal law banning payment for 'bone marrow' also ban payment for stem cells collected from a donor's blood using a modern process called apheresis?
cases.answer: No, the court ruled that stem cells collected via apheresis are part of the 'blood,' which is exempt from the payment ban, not 'bone marrow' itself.
cases.why: This case demonstrates how a narrow statutory interpretation, focusing on the precise words of a law, can create crucial distinctions that either permit or prohibit the commodification of valuable bodily materials.

tensions: Individual Autonomy vs. Public Good: The desire of individuals to control and profit from their own bodies ([[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] dissent) clashes with the public interest in promoting life-saving medical research and avoiding the commodification of human life ([[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] majority).

Commodification vs. Dignity: Should the law allow a market for human body parts? [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] and [[Flynn v. Holder]] show deep judicial and legislative reluctance, fearing exploitation and a loss of human dignity. [[Hecht v. Superior Court]], however, treats sperm as property to honor the decedent's procreative intent.

Legislature vs. Courts: Who should decide these novel property questions? The [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] majority explicitly states the legislature is better equipped to handle the complex policy issues of commercializing human tissue, while the [[Hecht v. Superior Court]] court steps in where the legislature has been silent.
traps: Overstating [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]]: Don't say [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] holds there are *no* property rights in the body. The holding is narrow: no cause of action for *conversion* of *excised cells* in that specific context. The informed consent claim succeeded, protecting the patient's right to autonomy.

Confusing [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] and [[Hecht v. Superior Court]]: [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] denied a property right in cells for commercial exploitation, while [[Hecht v. Superior Court]] found a property right in gametes for procreation. The key distinction is the *purpose* and *potential* of the biological material (research vs. reproduction).

Ignoring Statutory Language: In [[Flynn v. Holder]], the outcome turned entirely on the specific words of NOTA ('bone marrow,' 'subpart thereof,' and the exclusion of 'blood'). On an exam, if a statute is provided, its precise text is paramount, not just general policy arguments.
persons_commodities.exam_tip: When you see an issue involving human body parts, first ask: what is the material (e.g., regenerative cells, non-regenerative organ, gametes)? Second, what is the proposed use (e.g., research, transplant, procreation)? The law treats these differently. [[Hecht v. Superior Court]] protects procreative intent, while [[Moore v. Regents of the University of California]] and [[Flynn v. Holder]] limit commercial exploitation.

communities_customs_public_rights_water.summary: This unit explores how property rights are shaped and limited by sources outside of individual ownership, such as community custom, public trust, and statutory protections for cultural heritage. It focuses on resources that are inherently shared or have public significance, like wildlife, water, and cultural artifacts.

rules.rule: A landowner has a superior property right to wild animals (and their products) found on their land against a trespasser who discovers or captures them (ratione soli).

In many eastern states, owners of land bordering a watercourse (riparian owners) have a right to the reasonable use of the water, balancing their needs against those of other riparian owners. Natural wants (e.g., drinking) have priority over artificial wants (e.g., manufacturing).
Where the general rule of capture is impractical, a well-established and reasonable industry custom can determine ownership of a wild animal.

In many arid western states, the first person to divert water and put it to a beneficial use acquires a senior right to that water, regardless of whether they own land on the watercourse ('first in time, first in right').
Under the Public Trust Doctrine, states hold title to lands under navigable waters in trust for the public and cannot grant substantial portions to private parties in a way that abdicates this trust.
A long-standing, reasonable, certain, and uninterrupted public use of private land can create a public right of access based on the doctrine of custom, particularly for unique areas like beaches.

An overlying owner may make reasonable use of the percolating groundwater beneath their land for purposes beneficial to the land, but may not withdraw it for sale elsewhere if it injures neighboring landowners.

Under NAGPRA, objects of ongoing, central cultural importance to a tribe are 'cultural patrimony' and are inalienable by individuals, creating a form of communal ownership that overrides individual transactions.

cases.question: Does a person who finds a swarm of bees in a tree on another's land and marks the tree acquire property in the honey?
cases.answer: No, the landowner owns the honey by the principle of *ratione soli*, and a trespasser cannot acquire property rights through their wrongful act of trespass.
cases.why: This case establishes the strength of a landowner's right to exclude and to the resources found on their land, which trumps a trespasser's claim based on discovery.

cases.question: Can an upstream factory owner divert an entire stream for his use, depriving a downstream factory owner of water?
cases.answer: No, under the reasonable use doctrine, all riparian proprietors have a right to use the water for 'artificial' wants like manufacturing, and must share it when supply is limited.
cases.why: This case establishes the 'reasonable use' doctrine for riparian water rights in the eastern U.S., which balances the correlative rights of all landowners along a stream.

cases.question: Does a whaler who kills a whale with a marked bomb-lance own it, even if someone else finds the carcass washed ashore days later?
cases.answer: Yes, the court upheld a widely accepted and necessary industry custom to establish ownership when the normal rule of physical possession is impractical.
cases.why: This case shows that custom can be a valid source of property law, especially when it is essential to the survival of an industry and provides a workable rule where the common law is silent or unhelpful.

cases.question: In an arid region, who has a better right to water: the first person to divert it for farming, or a downstream landowner on the same creek?
cases.answer: The first appropriator has the prior right, because the common law of riparian rights is unsuited to arid climates where irrigation is an 'imperative necessity.'
cases.why: This case establishes the 'prior appropriation' doctrine of western water law, a fundamentally different system based on productive use ('first in time, first in right'), not land location.

cases.question: Can a state legislature grant a private railroad company permanent ownership of Chicago's entire commercial waterfront?
cases.answer: No, the state holds submerged lands under navigable waters in a 'public trust' for the people and cannot abdicate its control over such a vital public resource.
cases.why: This is the foundational U.S. Supreme Court case for the Public Trust Doctrine, a powerful limit on government power that prevents the privatization of essential public resources like navigable waters.

cases.question: Can oceanfront property owners fence off the dry-sand portion of the beach that the public has used for recreation for as long as anyone can remember?
cases.answer: No, the court held that the public had acquired a recreational easement over the dry-sand area through the ancient English doctrine of custom.
cases.why: This case shows how long-standing, uninterrupted, and reasonable public use can create a permanent public property right on private land, severely limiting the owner's right to exclude.

cases.question: Can a city pump vast amounts of groundwater from under rural land to sell in the city, if doing so will dry up the farmers' land?
cases.answer: No, the court adopted the 'reasonable use' rule for groundwater, which prohibits transporting it for use off-site if it harms neighboring landowners who rely on it for their own land.
cases.why: This case shows the evolution of common law, as the court rejected the old 'absolute ownership' rule for groundwater in favor of a modern 'reasonable use' rule that protects the correlative rights of neighbors.

cases.question: Is the federal law (NAGPRA) defining certain Native American items as inalienable 'cultural patrimony' too vague to be enforced against a dealer who tries to sell sacred masks?
cases.answer: No, the court found the definition was not unconstitutionally vague, especially as applied to a knowledgeable dealer who understood the items were communally important and not meant to be sold.
cases.why: This case affirms the concept of inalienable communal property, where an object's cultural importance to a group makes it legally impossible for any individual, even a tribal member, to sell it.

tensions: Private Rights vs. Public Interest: Private ownership is limited by public rights derived from custom ([[State ex rel. Thornton v. Hay]]), public trust ([[Illinois Central Railroad Co. v. Illinois]]), and the needs of a community for shared resources ([[Evans v. Merriweather]], [[Higday v. Nickolaus]]).

Formal Law vs. Custom: When should informal, community-based rules be recognized as law? [[Ghen v. Rich]] and [[State ex rel. Thornton v. Hay]] embrace custom as a source of property rights, while [[Fisher v. Steward]] rejects a local usage in favor of formal trespass rules.

East vs. West (Water Law): The difference between [[Evans v. Merriweather]] (riparian rights) and [[Coffin v. Left Hand Ditch Co.]] (prior appropriation) illustrates a major geographical split in American property law, driven entirely by environmental conditions (water scarcity).

Individual vs. Communal Ownership: [[United States v. Corrow]] introduces 'cultural patrimony,' where an object belongs to a culture itself and cannot be alienated by an individual. This clashes with the Western concept of property as a bundle of rights held by an individual, including the right to sell.
traps: Applying the Wrong Water Rule: The biggest trap is applying riparian rights ([[Evans v. Merriweather]]) to a fact pattern set in an arid western state, or prior appropriation ([[Coffin v. Left Hand Ditch Co.]]) to one in a place like Illinois. The location is critical. If not specified, analyze under both.

Confusing Custom and Prescription: In [[State ex rel. Thornton v. Hay]], the court chose custom over prescription. Custom applies to the public in a locality and is based on ancient, reasonable use. Prescription is more like adverse possession and can be harder to prove for the public as a whole.

Misunderstanding the Public Trust Doctrine: The doctrine in [[Illinois Central Railroad Co. v. Illinois]] doesn't prevent *all* grants of submerged land. States can grant small parcels for uses that aid public commerce (like building a pier). It prohibits large-scale grants that abdicate the state's control over a public resource.

Ignoring Trespass: In first possession scenarios, remember [[Fisher v. Steward]]. A claim based on discovery can be defeated if the claimant was trespassing. The landowner's right *ratione soli* is a powerful counter-argument to a trespasser's claim.
communities_customs_public_rights_water.exam_tip: When an issue involves a shared or public-facing resource (water, beaches, cultural items), don't just analyze the rights of the immediate parties. Ask: Is there a broader community interest at stake? Look for facts suggesting long-standing public use ([[State ex rel. Thornton v. Hay]]), a vital industry practice ([[Ghen v. Rich]]), a navigable waterway ([[Illinois Central Railroad Co. v. Illinois]]), or an item of deep cultural significance ([[United States v. Corrow]]). These facts trigger doctrines that can override individual claims.

4. Owner Sovereignty and Its Limits.intro: This chapter explores the limits of an owner’s power. While ownership grants the right to exclude and control, this “owner sovereignty” is not absolute. The law curtails it to prevent violence, protect public interests, and resolve disputes equitably. The units examine these limits through different lenses. The first explores when self-help is forbidden in favor of judicial process and when common law defenses like necessity can override an owner’s right to exclude. The second delves into equity’s power to constrain an owner’s rights, such as the right to destroy property or demand removal of minor encroachments. The third looks at how owners voluntarily limit their own sovereignty through consensual arrangements like licenses and bailments. This chapter directly addresses the course’s central question: what beats ownership? The answer includes public safety, necessity, equity, and contract.

criminal_law_self_help_common_law_defens.summary: This unit examines the significant legal restrictions on an owner's right to use self-help to enforce property rights, favoring judicial process to prevent violence. It also covers common law privileges, like necessity, that can justify what would otherwise be a trespass.

rules.rule: Modern Rule on Eviction: A landlord may not use self-help to dispossess a tenant who has not abandoned or surrendered the premises; the landlord must use judicial process.
UCC Self-Help Repossession: A secured party may repossess collateral without judicial process if it can be done without a “breach of the peace.”

Breach of the Peace: Repossession breaches the peace if it involves force, threats, or a real risk of violence. In [[Williams v. Ford Motor Credit Co.]] (Arkansas law) a 4:30 a.m. driveway repossession was lawful because the debtor did not object or resist and the agents were polite; under the usual rule, a clear objection at the scene means the creditor must stop and go to court.

Trespass to Chattels (Digital): Under California law, sending unsolicited emails to a company's server is not a trespass to chattels unless it causes actual physical damage or functional impairment to the computer system itself.
Doctrine of Necessity: Necessity, especially to preserve human life, can justify an interference with another’s property that would otherwise be a trespass. An owner may not repel such an entry.

Wrongful self-help by a mistaken improver: a building put on another's land belongs to the landowner by accession, so a builder who maliciously tears it down loses any equitable claim and must pay for the destroyed house (plus punitive damages).
cases: [[Producers Lumber & Supply Co. v. Olney Building Co.]]

cases.question: Can a dock owner be held liable for unmooring a boat that tied up to the dock without permission during a dangerous storm?
cases.answer: Ploof (boat owner) won because the doctrine of necessity gave him a privilege to trespass on the dock to save his life and property, making the dock owner's removal of the boat wrongful.
cases.why: This case establishes that the right to exclude is not absolute and can be overcome by the privilege of private necessity, especially when human life is at risk.

cases.case: [[Producers Lumber & Supply Co. v. Olney Building Co.]]
cases.question: Can a company that mistakenly builds a house on the wrong lot, and then demolishes it after failing to reach a settlement, be held liable for the value of the destroyed house?
cases.answer: Producers Lumber (landowner) won: the house had become the landowner's property by accession, and the builder's malicious demolition gave it unclean hands, so it owed the value of the house plus punitive damages instead of getting equitable relief.
cases.why: This case shows that self-help is strongly disfavored; a mistaken improver must seek relief in court and cannot take the law into their own hands by destroying the improvement.

cases.question: Can a landlord legally change the locks on a commercial tenant who the landlord believes has breached the lease, or must the landlord go to court?
cases.answer: Berg (tenant) won because the court adopted the modern rule that a landlord must always use judicial process to evict a tenant in possession and cannot use self-help, even if the reentry is 'peaceable.'
cases.why: This case marks a definitive shift away from the common law right of self-help for landlords, prioritizing the prevention of potential violence over the landlord's expediency.

cases.question: Does repossessing a car from a driveway at 4:30 a.m., over the owner's verbal objection but without threats or force, constitute a 'breach of the peace'?
cases.answer: Ford Motor Credit Co. (creditor) won because the repossession was accomplished without any incident that might provoke violence; the owner did not physically resist and the agents were polite.
cases.why: This case defines the limits of permissible self-help under the UCC, setting a high bar for what constitutes a 'breach of the peace' that requires more than just the owner's objection.

cases.question: Does sending unwanted mass emails to a company's employees, which cause no damage to the computer system but distract employees, constitute a trespass to chattels?
cases.answer: Hamidi (sender) won because trespass to chattels requires some actual injury to the chattel itself (the computer system), not just economic harm resulting from the content of the messages.
cases.why: This case shows courts' reluctance to apply traditional real property trespass rules to the digital world, requiring actual impairment of the system rather than just an unwanted intrusion.

tensions: Self-Help vs. Judicial Process: The law strongly prefers court action to prevent violence ([[Berg v. Wiley]]) but carves out exceptions where self-help is deemed efficient and less likely to cause conflict, such as UCC repossession ([[Williams v. Ford Motor Credit Co.]]).

Defining 'Breach of the Peace': There is a tension between a rule that requires actual violence or threats (the majority in [[Williams v. Ford Motor Credit Co.]]) and one that would require a repossessor to retreat at any sign of confrontation to avoid the *risk* of violence (the dissent's view).

Absolute Right to Exclude vs. Necessity: An owner's fundamental right to exclude is powerful, but not absolute. It can be temporarily suspended by a privilege of necessity to prevent greater harm, especially to human life ([[Ploof v. Putnam]]).

Applying Old Torts to New Technology: Courts struggle with whether to treat digital 'property' like physical property. [[Intel Corp. v. Hamidi]] refused to treat a server like land, declining to find a trespass without physical harm, fearing it would stifle communication.
traps: Applying the wrong landlord-tenant rule. Do not apply the old common law rule allowing 'peaceable' self-help eviction. [[Berg v. Wiley]] establishes the modern majority rule: landlords must use the judicial process (summary eviction proceedings).

Misinterpreting 'breach of the peace.' It isn't limited to a fistfight. Ask whether the repossession created a risk of violence, and whether the debtor clearly objected at the scene (if so, most courts require the creditor to stop). In [[Williams v. Ford Motor Credit Co.]] the debtor did not object; the dissent thought a pre-dawn confrontation was risky enough anyway.

Assuming necessity is a free pass. The privilege in [[Ploof v. Putnam]] allows entry to avoid a trespass claim, but it does not resolve whether the person entering is liable for any actual damage they cause to the property. Note this as an open question.

Equating mistaken improvement with a right to remove. A good-faith improver may get equitable relief (payment, a forced sale, removal at its own cost), but it has no right to destroy the improvement on its own; doing so is wrongful ([[Producers Lumber & Supply Co. v. Olney Building Co.]]).
criminal_law_self_help_common_law_defens.exam_tip: When you see a party using self-help (e.g., a landlord changing locks, a creditor towing a car, an improver demolishing a building), analyze its legality. For landlords, it's wrongful ([[Berg v. Wiley]]). For secured creditors, it's a 'breach of the peace' analysis ([[Williams v. Ford Motor Credit Co.]]). For mistaken improvers, self-help destruction is wrongful ([[Producers Lumber & Supply Co. v. Olney Building Co.]]). Always state the strong policy preference for judicial process over self-help to prevent violence.

equity_abandonment_destruction.summary: This unit explores the power of equity to limit an owner's rights. Courts may balance hardships to deny injunctions for minor encroachments, prevent the wasteful destruction of property, and refuse to allow abandonment of real property, all in the service of fairness and public policy.

rules.rule: Strict Rule on Encroachment (Minority View): An owner has an absolute right to an injunction ordering the removal of an encroaching structure, no matter how small the encroachment or how great the cost of removal.

Relative Hardship Doctrine (Majority View): A court may deny a mandatory injunction to remove a minor, unintentional encroachment if the cost of removal is grossly disproportionate to the harm caused, relegating the plaintiff to damages.

Right to Destroy: A testamentary direction to destroy valuable property may be voided as against public policy if it is capricious, serves no legitimate purpose, and causes significant harm to the estate, neighbors, and the community.

Abandonment of Real Property: Under Pennsylvania law, real property owned in fee simple with perfect title cannot be abandoned. The owner remains liable for all associated obligations (e.g., taxes, HOA fees).
