Unjust Enrichment ('Waiver of Tort'): When a tortfeasor benefits from the wrongful use of another's property, the owner may sue for restitution of the benefit (the tortfeasor's profits or savings), even if the owner suffered no direct loss.

Four-Factor Injunction Test: To obtain a permanent injunction, a plaintiff must demonstrate (1) irreparable injury, (2) inadequacy of legal remedies, (3) a balance of hardships favoring the plaintiff, and (4) that the public interest is not disserved. This test applies in all contexts, including patent law.

Equity's discretion: an injunction is never automatic. A court may deny one and leave the plaintiff to damages where the plaintiff bought land knowing of the harm, as a speculation, and money fully compensates the loss.

cases.question: Should a court grant an injunction to stop a mining company from polluting a downstream property if the owner bought the land specifically to force the company to buy it from him at an inflated price?
cases.answer: Allouez Mining (defendant) won on the injunction: Edwards bought the land knowing of the sand dumping, as a speculation, so damages fully compensated him and equity declined to add an injunction.
cases.why: This case shows that a plaintiff's motive and conduct can be critical in equity; a court may deny an injunction if the plaintiff is not acting in good faith.

cases.question: Must a defendant remove a foundation that unintentionally encroaches 1 and 3/8 inches onto a neighbor's land, even if the only way to do so is to tear down their entire wall?
cases.answer: Pile (plaintiff) won because the court held that the defendants had no right to occupy land that was not theirs, enforcing the plaintiff's absolute right to exclude regardless of the hardship to the defendant.
cases.why: This case represents the traditional, strict 'property rule' approach, prioritizing the landowner's absolute right to exclude over equitable considerations of cost or intent.

cases.question: Can the owner of a machine recover the profits a defendant made by using it without permission, even though the owner wasn't using the machine and suffered no direct financial loss?
cases.answer: Olwell (plaintiff) won because he could 'waive the tort' of conversion and sue for restitution based on unjust enrichment, allowing him to recover the benefit the defendant gained from the wrongful use.
cases.why: This case establishes that the right to exclusive use is itself a valuable property right, and a remedy for its violation can be measured by the defendant's gain, not just the plaintiff's loss.

cases.question: Must a defendant remove a building foundation that unintentionally encroaches a few inches underground if the cost of removal is huge and the harm to the plaintiff is minimal?
cases.answer: Golden Press (defendant) won because the court applied the 'relative hardship' doctrine, denying an injunction where the encroachment was in good faith, the harm was slight, and the cost of removal was unconscionable.
cases.why: This case represents the modern, 'liability rule' approach to minor encroachments, where courts balance the equities rather than automatically granting an injunction, and may award damages instead.

cases.question: Can a court block the execution of a will that directs the executor to raze a valuable, historic house for no apparent reason?
cases.answer: The neighbors won because the court found the direction to destroy the house was void as against public policy, as it was a capricious, senseless act that harmed the estate, the neighbors, and the community.
cases.why: This case establishes a major limit on the right to destroy property, showing that owner autonomy, especially post-mortem, can be overridden by public policy concerns about waste and community harm.

cases.question: Can a landowner abandon a useless plot of land to stop having to pay taxes and homeowners' association fees?
cases.answer: The Association won because Pennsylvania law does not permit the abandonment of real property held in fee simple; title remains with the owner until it is transferred to another party.
cases.why: This case establishes a bright-line rule that you cannot simply 'walk away' from the obligations of real property ownership; the duties of title are inescapable through abandonment.

cases.question: Should a court automatically grant a permanent injunction after a patent has been found to be valid and infringed?
cases.answer: The Supreme Court held that there is no automatic injunction for patent infringement; courts must apply the traditional four-factor test for equitable relief on a case-by-case basis.
cases.why: This case rejects categorical rules for injunctions in property disputes, confirming that injunctive relief is an equitable remedy subject to judicial discretion, even for a core property right like a patent's right to exclude.

tensions: Property Rules vs. Liability Rules: When should a court protect an entitlement with an injunction (a property rule, as in [[Pile v. Pedrick]]) versus allowing the infringement to continue but awarding damages (a liability rule, as in [[Golden Press Inc. v. Rylands]])? The modern trend favors balancing hardships and using liability rules for unintentional, minor harms.

Owner Autonomy vs. Public Policy: How far does an owner's right to do what they want with their property extend? [[Eyerman v. Mercantile Trust Co.]] shows the right to destroy is limited by public policy against waste, while [[Pocono Springs Civic Association v. MacKenzie]] shows the obligations of ownership cannot be shirked through abandonment.

The Role of Motive in Equity: Should a plaintiff's 'bad' motive, like the speculative intent in [[Edwards v. Allouez Mining Co.]], bar them from receiving an equitable remedy like an injunction? This creates a tension between protecting property rights absolutely and ensuring that equitable remedies are used for equitable purposes.
traps: Assuming an injunction is automatic for trespass. After [[Golden Press Inc. v. Rylands]] and [[eBay Inc. v. MercExchange L.L.C.]], you must apply a balancing test. For an encroachment, analyze the relative hardship. Is the encroachment minor and in good faith? Is the cost of removal grossly disproportionate to the harm? Argue both the strict [[Pile v. Pedrick]] rule and the modern balancing approach.

Confusing abandonment of personal vs. real property. You can abandon a chair by leaving it on the curb, but [[Pocono Springs Civic Association v. MacKenzie]] shows you cannot abandon a plot of land held in fee simple to escape taxes or HOA fees. Title is sticky.

Forgetting the unjust enrichment remedy. If a trespasser uses property but causes no physical damage (e.g., lives in a vacant house for a month), don't conclude there's no remedy. The owner can sue for the benefit the trespasser received (the fair rental value) under the theory of unjust enrichment from [[Olwell v. Nye & Nissen Co.]].
equity_abandonment_destruction.exam_tip: When you see a continuing trespass like an encroachment or pollution, the key issue is the remedy. Don't just identify the tort; analyze whether the plaintiff can get an injunction. Argue both sides: the plaintiff's absolute right to exclude ([[Pile v. Pedrick]]) versus an equitable balancing of the hardships ([[Golden Press Inc. v. Rylands]]). The defendant's state of mind (willful vs. good faith) and the plaintiff's conduct (delay, or buying into the harm as a speculation as in [[Edwards v. Allouez Mining Co.]]) are critical factors in the analysis.

licenses_bailments.summary: This unit covers temporary transfers of property rights. It distinguishes between bailments (transfer of possession creating a duty of care) and licenses (mere permission to use), and explores how modern commercial practices like 'park-and-lock' garages and 'shrinkwrap' software licenses fit into these traditional categories.

rules.rule: Implied Bailment in Garages: A bailment for hire may be implied when a person parks in an enclosed, attended commercial garage, even if they lock the car and keep the keys. The operator's control over entry and exit is key.

Presumption of Bailee Negligence: In a bailment for hire, if the bailor proves delivery and the bailee's failure to return the property, a presumption of negligence arises, and the burden shifts to the bailee to prove they exercised due care.

Involuntary Bailee Liability: An involuntary bailee (one who comes into possession by mistake) has a minimal duty of care. However, if they exercise dominion over the property (e.g., by attempting to return it), they assume the strict liability of a voluntary bailee for misdelivery.

Voluntary Bailee Strict Liability for Misdelivery: A voluntary bailee has an absolute duty to redeliver the property to the rightful owner. Good faith or lack of negligence is not an excuse for misdelivery.

Enforceability of Shrinkwrap Licenses: A shrinkwrap license is an enforceable contract if the buyer accepts the goods by using them after having an opportunity to read the terms and reject the contract by returning the product for a refund.

Copyright Preemption and Contracts: Private contractual rights that are not 'equivalent' to exclusive rights under copyright are not preempted by the Copyright Act. Contracts bind only the parties and are not rights against the world.

cases.question: When a stockbroker mistakenly receives the wrong bond and then, in a good-faith attempt to return it, hands it to the wrong messenger who absconds with it, is the broker liable for its value?
cases.answer: The plaintiffs (senders) won because the defendant broker, by exercising dominion over the bond in attempting to return it, became an involuntary bailee with the same strict liability for misdelivery as a voluntary bailee.
cases.why: This case establishes that exercising dominion over property, even as an involuntary bailee, triggers a high level of responsibility, including absolute liability for delivering it to the wrong person.

cases.question: Is the operator of a commercial 'park and lock' garage liable when a customer's car is stolen, even though the customer kept the keys?
cases.answer: Allen (customer) won because the court found an implied bailment for hire was created due to the garage's control over the premises (enclosed, attended exit), which gave rise to a presumption of negligence that the hotel failed to rebut.
cases.why: This case adapts the traditional concept of bailment to modern commercial settings, focusing on the operator's control and the customer's reasonable expectations of security rather than the physical transfer of keys.

cases.question: Is a 'shrinkwrap license' inside a software box, which limits use to non-commercial purposes, an enforceable contract against a buyer who ignores the terms?
cases.answer: ProCD (vendor) won because the court held that the license was an enforceable contract formed when the user, after having an opportunity to read the terms, kept and used the software instead of returning it for a refund.
cases.why: This landmark case validated the 'pay now, terms later' model of contract formation for software and other goods, emphasizing freedom of contract and its role in protecting intellectual property outside of copyright law.

tensions: Bailment vs. License: The line between a bailment (transfer of possession and control) and a license (mere permission to use) is blurry in modern contexts. The key factor is the degree of control exercised by the property owner, as seen in the majority and dissenting opinions in [[Allen v. Hyatt Regency-Nashville Hotel]].

Strict Liability vs. Negligence for Bailees: Should a bailee who makes an honest mistake and misdelivers property be held strictly liable for conversion ([[Cowen v. Pressprich]] majority), or should they only be liable if they were negligent (the dissent's view)? The law imposes a very high, strict duty to ensure property is returned to its true owner.

Freedom of Contract vs. Federal IP Law: To what extent can private contracts create property-like protections for information that federal law leaves unprotected? [[ProCD Inc. v. Zeidenberg]] shows that contract law provides a powerful tool for owners to control the use of their intellectual assets, operating alongside but separate from copyright.
traps: Assuming 'park and lock' is always a license. It's a fact-intensive inquiry. [[Allen v. Hyatt Regency-Nashville Hotel]] found a bailment due to the garage's control (enclosed, attended exit). On an exam, contrast this with an open, unattended lot, which would likely be a license. Analyze the facts to argue both sides.

Ignoring the two stages of involuntary bailment. When someone accidentally receives property, they are an involuntary bailee. At first, their duty is minimal. The critical moment is when they 'exercise dominion.' As in [[Cowen v. Pressprich]], even a well-intentioned act like trying to return the item can trigger the strict liability of a voluntary bailee for misdelivery.

Thinking copyright law voids all contrary license terms. [[ProCD Inc. v. Zeidenberg]] shows that contracts can create rights separate from copyright. A license can validly prohibit conduct that copyright law might otherwise permit (e.g., copying unoriginal facts for commercial use), because contract rights are personal between the parties and not preempted.
licenses_bailments.exam_tip: When you see one person holding another's property, first classify the relationship. Is it a bailment or a license? The key is control. If it's a bailment, determine the standard of care. For a 'park and lock' fact pattern, argue both bailment and license, using the facts to show the degree of control exercised by the operator ([[Allen v. Hyatt Regency-Nashville Hotel]]). For digital goods, analyze contract formation: did the user have notice of the terms and an opportunity to reject them ([[ProCD Inc. v. Zeidenberg]])?

6. Entity Property.intro: This chapter explores how property rights are structured when ownership is held not by a single person but by an entity. We begin with the landlord-tenant relationship, a foundational entity form, examining traditional rules and the modern shift toward contract principles. This sets the stage for more complex entities like condominiums, cooperatives, and trusts. The units fit together by showing a progression from the two-person landlord-tenant entity to multi-party common interest communities and fiduciary relationships. The chapter addresses the course's central question by demonstrating how joining an entity—whether as a tenant, condo owner, or beneficiary—fragments the classic bundle of rights. Individual owner sovereignty is often curtailed by leases, bylaws, and fiduciary duties, showing that the collective good or a fiduciary's obligation can 'beat' an individual's ownership claims.

leases_traditional_rules.summary: This unit covers the traditional landlord-tenant relationship, focusing on the landlord's duty to provide quiet enjoyment and the tenant's remedy of constructive eviction. It also examines a commercial landlord's options when a tenant repudiates the lease.

rules.rule: A tenant is constructively evicted when a landlord's action or inaction substantially deprives them of the quiet enjoyment of the premises, and the tenant vacates within a reasonable time.

A landlord can be held responsible for a nuisance created by another tenant if the landlord had the ability to control the objectionable conditions and their actions were a natural and probable consequence of permitting the nuisance-creating activity.
In determining a breach of the implied warranty of quiet enjoyment, the landlord's conduct, not their subjective intent, is the controlling factor.

Upon a commercial tenant's repudiation, a landlord may: (1) reject the repudiation and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; (2) re-let on the tenant's behalf; or (3) accept the surrender and re-let for its own account, terminating the tenant's future liability.

A landlord's acceptance of a tenant's surrender may occur 'by operation of law' through actions inconsistent with the continuation of the tenancy (e.g., re-letting for the landlord's sole benefit), even if the landlord previously rejected the surrender.
In some jurisdictions (like New York), a commercial landlord has no duty to mitigate damages after a tenant's repudiation.

cases.question: Can a landlord be held responsible for a breach of quiet enjoyment due to extreme noise from another tenant?
cases.answer: Yes, the landlords breached the implied warranty of quiet enjoyment because they leased to a disruptive commercial tenant and had the power to control the noise but failed to do so.
cases.why: This case expands landlord liability for constructive eviction to include failure to control a nuisance created by a third party, if the landlord has the power to control it.

cases.question: Can a landlord's actions to re-let a property for their own benefit be considered an acceptance of the tenant's surrender, even if the landlord verbally rejected it?
cases.answer: Yes, the landlord's active efforts to re-lease the property for their own account were inconsistent with the original tenancy and constituted an acceptance of surrender by operation of law, ending the tenant's liability for future rent.
cases.why: It demonstrates that a landlord's conduct can override their stated intentions, creating a 'surrender by operation of law' that terminates the lease and the tenant's ongoing obligations.

tensions: Landlord's Duty vs. Tenant's Rights: How far does a landlord's duty to control one tenant's behavior extend before it infringes on that tenant's right to use their leased property? [[Blackett v. Olanoff]] highlights this conflict.

Formalism vs. Realism in Surrender: Should a landlord's explicit rejection of surrender be legally binding, or should courts look to the reality of their subsequent actions (like trying to re-let for their own benefit) to find an implied acceptance? [[Gotlieb v. Taco Bell Corp.]] favors realism.

Commercial vs. Residential Leases: The rule in [[Gotlieb v. Taco Bell Corp.]] that commercial landlords may have no duty to mitigate damages stands in stark contrast to modern reforms in residential leases, raising policy questions about whether sophisticated commercial parties require fewer protections.
traps: Forgetting the 'Vacate' Requirement: A claim of constructive eviction fails if the tenant does not actually vacate the premises within a reasonable time after the landlord's breach. Staying and suing for damages is a different remedy.

Misunderstanding Surrender: A tenant cannot unilaterally terminate a lease by abandoning the property. A 'surrender' requires acceptance by the landlord, either explicitly or 'by operation of law' through the landlord's actions. [[Gotlieb v. Taco Bell Corp.]].

Assuming a Duty to Mitigate: Do not automatically assume a landlord must mitigate damages, especially in a commercial lease. State the majority rule (duty to mitigate) and the minority/traditional rule (no duty to mitigate) and note that jurisdictions like New York in [[Gotlieb v. Taco Bell Corp.]] follow the latter for commercial leases.
leases_traditional_rules.exam_tip: When a tenant leaves before the lease term ends, first determine the reason. If it's due to a condition on the premises, analyze for breach of quiet enjoyment and constructive eviction ([[Blackett v. Olanoff]]). If the tenant simply walks away (repudiates), analyze the landlord's subsequent actions to see if they constitute an acceptance of surrender ([[Gotlieb v. Taco Bell Corp.]]).

leases_reforms_transfers.summary: This unit explores the modernization of lease law, which increasingly treats leases as contracts rather than conveyances. Key developments include the implied warranty of habitability in residential leases and a shift toward enforcing the parties' intent in lease transfers.

rules.rule: Leases are viewed as having a dual character as both a conveyance and a contract, with modern courts emphasizing contract principles to give effect to the parties' intentions.

Covenants in a lease are dependent if they go to the entire consideration of the contract; a material breach of a dependent covenant by the landlord (e.g., an exclusive use clause) can justify the tenant's rescission of the lease.

The modern rule for distinguishing an assignment from a sublease is to ascertain the intention of the parties, rejecting the rigid common law test based on whether the transferor retained a reversionary interest.
A warranty of habitability (IWH), measured by the local housing code, is implied by law into urban residential leases. A landlord's breach of the IWH is a defense to an action for nonpayment of rent.
Under the IWH, a tenant's obligation to pay rent is dependent on the landlord's performance of their obligation to maintain a habitable premises.
For a lease covenant to 'run with the land' and bind a successor owner, it must 'touch and concern' the land by being so related to the land as to enhance its value or confer a benefit upon it.
cases: [[Mullendore Theatres Inc. v. Growth Realty Investors Co.]]

rules.rule: A landlord's covenant to refund a security deposit is generally a personal obligation that does not 'touch and concern' the land and therefore does not bind a successor landlord unless the lease restricts the use of the funds for the property's benefit.
cases: [[Mullendore Theatres Inc. v. Growth Realty Investors Co.]]

cases.question: Can a commercial tenant break a lease when the landlord breaches a promise not to rent to a competitor?
cases.answer: Yes, the tenant won because the landlord's promise was a material, dependent covenant, and its breach frustrated the entire purpose of the lease, justifying rescission.
cases.why: This case shows the move toward treating leases as contracts, where a material breach by one party can excuse performance by the other, rejecting the old rule that lease covenants were independent.

cases.question: Should a lease transfer be classified as an assignment or a sublease based on the parties' intent or on the old common law rule about retaining a reversion?
cases.answer: The court should follow the parties' intent, so the transfer was an assignment, and the promissory notes were for the sale of the lease, not rent that would terminate when the building burned down.
cases.why: This case explicitly rejects a rigid, feudal-era property rule in favor of a modern, contract-based approach that prioritizes the actual intent of the parties.

cases.question: Can tenants use numerous housing code violations as a defense against eviction for not paying rent?
cases.answer: Yes, the tenants won because the court established an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases, making the landlord's duty to maintain the premises and the tenant's duty to pay rent dependent on each other.
cases.why: This is a landmark case that revolutionized residential landlord-tenant law by importing contract principles (implied warranties, dependent obligations) and rejecting the old property doctrine of 'caveat emptor'.

cases.case: [[Mullendore Theatres Inc. v. Growth Realty Investors Co.]]
cases.question: Is a successor landlord obligated to refund a security deposit paid to the original landlord?
cases.answer: No, the successor landlord won because a covenant to refund a security deposit is a personal promise that does not 'touch and concern' the land, and therefore does not run with the land to bind successors.
cases.why: It provides a clear example of the 'touch and concern' test, demonstrating that not all promises in a lease automatically bind future owners of the property.

tensions: Property vs. Contract: This is the unit's central theme. Should leases be governed by old property rules (independent covenants, formal distinctions) or modern contract principles (dependent covenants, implied warranties, focus on intent)? [[Javins v. First National Realty Corp.]] and [[Jaber v. Miller]] champion the contract approach.

Intent vs. Formalism: Should the legal effect of a document depend on the parties' actual intent or on whether they used the correct legal formula (e.g., retaining a one-day reversion to create a sublease)? [[Jaber v. Miller]] favors intent over formalism.

Binding Successors: When should a promise made by a prior owner bind a new one? The 'touch and concern' test in [[Mullendore Theatres Inc. v. Growth Realty Investors Co.]] tries to draw a line between personal promises and those integral to the land itself, but this line can be difficult to apply.
traps: Applying IWH to Commercial Leases: The implied warranty of habitability from [[Javins v. First National Realty Corp.]] is for residential leases. Do not apply it to a commercial lease fact pattern; parties in a commercial context are presumed to be more sophisticated and able to contract for their own protections.

Mixing Up Assignment and Sublease Rules: On an exam, state both the modern (intent-based) rule from [[Jaber v. Miller]] and the traditional (reversion-based) common law rule. Analyze the facts under both and explain which rule the jurisdiction is likely to follow (most modern courts prefer the intent-based rule).

Assuming All Covenants Run: Just because a promise is in a lease does not mean it binds a successor owner. You must run the 'touch and concern' analysis. A simple promise to pay money, like a security deposit refund, is a classic example of a personal covenant that does not run. [[Mullendore Theatres Inc. v. Growth Realty Investors Co.]].
leases_reforms_transfers.exam_tip: When analyzing a landlord-tenant dispute, the first question is always: is this a residential or commercial lease? The answer is a crucial fork in the road, determining whether modern reforms like the IWH ([[Javins]]) apply or if more traditional contract rules ([[Medico-Dental]]) or even older property rules are more likely to govern.

entity_forms_condos_coops_corps_partners.summary: This unit examines how property rights are managed within collective entities like condos, co-ops, and trusts, focusing on the tension between an individual owner's autonomy and the power of the governing body to create and enforce rules for the collective good.

rules.rule: A fiduciary, such as an executor or trustee, owes an absolute duty of undivided loyalty and must avoid any self-dealing or conflicts of interest. A transaction tainted by a conflict is voidable without inquiry into its fairness.
A fiduciary who breaches the duty of loyalty may be liable for 'appreciation damages'—the value of the misappropriated property at the time of the court's decree.

The Business Judgment Rule: Courts will defer to the decisions of a cooperative board as long as the board acts for the purposes of the cooperative, within the scope of its authority, and in good faith.
cases: [[Levandusky v. One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.]]

rules.rule: Use restrictions contained in a condominium's recorded declaration (CC&Rs) are presumed reasonable and will be enforced unless they are arbitrary, violate a fundamental public policy, or their burdens on the land substantially outweigh their benefits to the development as a whole.
The reasonableness of a recorded use restriction is evaluated based on the community as a whole, not on the specific, non-disruptive circumstances of an individual homeowner.

The business judgment rule also governs a co-op board's decision to terminate a tenancy for objectionable conduct under the lease, so long as the board acted for the cooperative's purposes, within its authority and in good faith.

A homeowners association's Declaration is its 'constitution' for fundamental property rights and can only be amended by its specified (usually supermajority) vote. Bylaws, which govern procedure, cannot be used to impose new, substantive use restrictions not authorized by the Declaration.

cases.question: What is the proper measure of damages when estate executors breach their duty of loyalty through self-dealing?
cases.answer: The petitioners won; the executors and the galleries were liable for appreciation damages, meaning the value of the paintings at the time of trial, not just their value at the time of the wrongful sale.
cases.why: This case establishes the high bar for the fiduciary duty of loyalty and the severe penalty (appreciation damages) for its breach, designed to deter self-dealing and make the beneficiary whole.

cases.case: [[Levandusky v. One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.]]
cases.question: What standard of review should courts use when evaluating decisions made by a residential cooperative's board of directors?
cases.answer: The co-op won; courts should apply the deferential business judgment rule, upholding the board's decision as long as it acted in good faith, within its authority, and for a legitimate corporate purpose.
cases.why: This case establishes the governing standard for co-op board decisions, prioritizing the board's authority to manage the community over judicial second-guessing of its choices.

cases.question: Can a condo owner challenge a recorded pet restriction as 'unreasonable' because her specific pets are quiet and create no nuisance?
cases.answer: No, the association won because a recorded restriction is presumed valid and its reasonableness is judged against the development as a whole, not the particular facts of one owner.
cases.why: It creates a strong presumption of validity for recorded CC&Rs, making them very difficult for individual homeowners to challenge and promoting stability in common interest communities.

cases.question: Must a court independently find a co-op tenant's conduct 'objectionable,' or should it defer to the shareholder vote terminating the tenancy?
cases.answer: The co-op won; the court should apply the business judgment rule and defer to the cooperative's decision, as long as the board acted in good faith and within its authority.
cases.why: This case extends the highly deferential business judgment rule to the extreme sanction of tenancy termination, showing the significant power of a co-op board over individual property rights.

cases.question: Can a homeowners association impose new rental restrictions through a bylaw amendment when the Declaration is silent on the issue and requires a supermajority to amend?
cases.answer: No, the homeowners won because a fundamental property right restriction must be enacted by amending the Declaration according to its own rules, not through a more easily passed bylaw.
cases.why: It establishes a clear hierarchy for governing documents, protecting fundamental property rights defined in the Declaration from being easily altered by a simple majority via the bylaws.

tensions: Individual Rights vs. Collective Good: The central tension of the unit. How much individual freedom must an owner sacrifice for the stability and harmony of a common interest community? Compare the individual's loss in [[Nahrstedt v. Lakeside Village Condominium Association]] with the community's gain in stability.

Judicial Deference vs. Judicial Oversight: The business judgment rule ([[Levandusky v. One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.]], [[40 West 67th Street v. Pullman]]) signals strong deference to boards, while strict enforcement of the governing documents' amendment procedures ([[Kiekel v. Four Colonies Homes Association]]) keeps a role for courts.

Fiduciary Power vs. Fiduciary Duty: Entities grant fiduciaries (trustees, board members) immense power over property. The law constrains that power with strict duties of loyalty and care, with [[In re Estate of Rothko]] showing the severe consequences when that duty is breached.
traps: Confusing Condos and Co-ops: In a condo, you own real property (your unit). In a co-op, you own personal property (shares in a corporation) and have a proprietary lease. This landlord-tenant relationship in co-ops helps explain the board's extensive power, as seen in [[40 West 67th Street v. Pullman]].

Applying the Wrong Standard of Review: For a board's discretionary *decision*, use the business judgment rule ([[Levandusky]]). For a pre-existing *recorded restriction* in the CC&Rs, use the 'unreasonable' test ([[Nahrstedt]]). For a *new rule*, check if it was passed properly according to the hierarchy of governing documents ([[Kiekel]]).

Arguing Fairness in a Self-Dealing Case: Don't waste time arguing that a fiduciary's self-dealing transaction was 'fair.' The 'no further inquiry' rule from [[In re Estate of Rothko]] means the transaction is voidable simply because of the conflict of interest, regardless of the price or terms.
entity_forms_condos_coops_corps_partners.exam_tip: When analyzing a dispute in a common interest community, first identify the source of the contested rule. Is it (1) a pre-existing restriction in the recorded Declaration/CC&Rs? (2) a discretionary decision by the board? or (3) a new rule passed via an amendment? The source dictates the standard of review: (1) [[Nahrstedt]]'s reasonableness test, (2) [[Levandusky]]'s business judgment rule, or (3) [[Kiekel]]'s hierarchy of documents analysis.

7. Security Interests.intro: This chapter examines security interests, a creditor's right in a debtor's property to secure repayment of a loan. This is a core exception to the owner's sovereignty. If the owner-debtor defaults, the creditor's interest 'beats' the owner's, allowing the creditor to force a sale of the property to satisfy the debt. The units explore the two most common real property security devices: the mortgage and the land sale contract. The cases show how courts, using principles of equity, limit a creditor's power to enforce their security interest. This protects the debtor's remaining value (their 'equity') in the property from being unfairly wiped out, balancing the creditor's right to be repaid against the owner's right to be treated fairly.

liens_mortgages.summary: A security interest, like a mortgage or a land sale contract, allows a creditor to take property upon default. However, courts impose equitable duties on creditors to protect the debtor's interest, often treating different security devices as functionally equivalent to a mortgage.

rules.rule: A conditional land sale contract is treated as a secured transaction analogous to a mortgage, where the vendor's legal title serves as a lien to secure the unpaid balance.
When a vendee under a land sale contract has acquired a substantial equitable interest, the vendor's remedy for default is judicial foreclosure, not enforcement of a contractual forfeiture clause.
Forfeiture of a land sale contract may be an appropriate remedy where the vendee has paid only a minimal amount, has abandoned the property, or is absconding.
A mortgagee executing a power of sale has a fiduciary-like duty to protect the mortgagor's interests by acting in good faith and with due diligence.

The duty of due diligence requires a mortgagee to exert every reasonable effort to obtain a 'fair and reasonable price under the circumstances,' which may require actions beyond mere statutory compliance, such as adjourning the sale or setting an upset price.
Inadequacy of price alone is not sufficient to demonstrate bad faith unless the price is so low as to shock the judicial conscience.
Damages for a mortgagee's lack of due diligence are the difference between a 'fair price' for the property and the price actually obtained at the foreclosure sale.

cases.question: Can a seller on a land sale contract keep all the buyer's payments and take back the property if the buyer defaults after paying a substantial portion of the price?
cases.answer: No, the buyer (Marshall) won; when a buyer has paid a substantial amount, the seller cannot enforce a forfeiture clause and must instead use judicial foreclosure, treating the contract like a mortgage.
cases.why: This case shows that courts will look past the form of a transaction (a 'land contract') to its substance (a 'secured transaction') to prevent an unfair forfeiture of the buyer's equity.

cases.question: Does a lender conducting a foreclosure sale have a duty to get a fair price for the property, beyond just following the statutory procedures?
cases.answer: Yes, the homeowner (Murphy) won on liability; a lender has a fiduciary-like duty of good faith and due diligence to get a fair price, and failing to do so can lead to damages.
cases.why: This case establishes that a lender's power of sale is not absolute; it is limited by an equitable duty to protect the borrower's equity, even if the lender follows all the technical rules.

tensions: Contract Freedom vs. Equity: Courts must balance the parties' freedom to agree on harsh remedies like forfeiture ([[Skendzel v. Marshall]]) against the equitable principle that the law 'abhors a forfeiture' and should intervene to prevent unconscionable losses.

Creditor Efficiency vs. Debtor Protection: The law provides creditors with efficient remedies like power of sale foreclosure, but [[Murphy v. Financial Development Corp.]] shows this efficiency is limited by duties of due diligence that protect the debtor's equity, potentially at the cost of a slower, more expensive process for the creditor.

Form vs. Substance: Should the name of the document ('Land Sale Contract' vs. 'Mortgage') determine the parties' rights? [[Skendzel v. Marshall]] prioritizes substance, treating the contract as a mortgage to prevent an inequitable result, reflecting a recurring theme in property law.
traps: Confusing Bad Faith and Lack of Due Diligence: A low foreclosure price does not automatically mean the lender acted in bad faith. Bad faith requires intent to harm, while a low price usually just shows a failure of due diligence. The distinction matters for damages, as [[Murphy v. Financial Development Corp.]] explains.

Assuming All Forfeiture Clauses Are Void: Don't over-read [[Skendzel v. Marshall]]. While it heavily disfavors forfeiture, it carves out exceptions. Forfeiture might be permitted if the buyer has paid very little, has abandoned the property, or is absconding. Always check how much equity the buyer has.

Ignoring Procedural Compliance: While [[Murphy v. Financial Development Corp.]] focuses on the equitable duty of due diligence, a creditor must first comply with all statutory foreclosure procedures (e.g., notice). A procedural error is a separate and often easier way to attack a sale. The equitable duties are *in addition to* statutory ones.

Miscalculating Damages: In a [[Murphy v. Financial Development Corp.]] scenario, remember the specific damage formulas. For lack of due diligence, damages are the difference between a 'fair price' and the sale price. For bad faith, it's the difference between 'fair market value' and the sale price. Fair market value is likely higher than a 'fair price' obtainable at a forced sale.
liens_mortgages.exam_tip: On an exam fact pattern involving a default, first identify the security device (mortgage, land sale contract). Then, analyze the creditor's remedy in two steps. (1) Procedure: Did the creditor follow all statutory rules for foreclosure? (2) Equity: Even if procedure was followed, did the creditor breach an equitable duty? For a mortgage, this is the duty of due diligence to get a fair price ([[Murphy v. Financial Development Corp.]]). For a land sale contract, it's the prohibition on forfeiture where the buyer has substantial equity ([[Skendzel v. Marshall]]).

8. Title Records and the Transfer of Pro.intro: This chapter examines how ownership of property is formally transferred and legally protected. It focuses on the vulnerabilities in the transfer process, particularly the conflict between an original owner and a subsequent good faith purchaser who buys without knowledge of prior claims. The unit on recording systems, good faith purchasers, and the distinction between void and voidable title directly addresses the course's central question: what beats ownership? It reveals that ownership is not absolute. A 'true' owner can lose their property to an innocent buyer if the owner was negligent, failed to provide public notice of their interest, or was tricked in a way that made the subsequent transfer possible, prioritizing market efficiency over the original owner's security.

title_transfer_land_transactions_good_fa.summary: This unit explains the rules governing title disputes between an original owner and a subsequent purchaser. It introduces the critical distinctions between void and voidable title and the conditions under which a bona fide purchaser can acquire good title from someone with a defective one.

rules.rule: Equitable Conversion: Upon signing an enforceable land sale contract, equitable title passes to the buyer, who assumes the risks of loss and benefits of appreciation. The seller retains legal title merely as security for the payment of the purchase price.

Void vs. Voidable Title (Goods): A thief who wrongfully takes goods has void title and cannot pass good title to anyone. A swindler who fraudulently induces a voluntary delivery of goods (e.g., with a bad check) acquires voidable title and has the power to transfer good title to a good faith purchaser for value.

Good Faith Purchaser (Goods): Under UCC § 2.403(a), a person with voidable title can transfer good title to a good faith purchaser for value. 'Good faith' is defined as 'honesty in fact,' but willful disregard of suspicious circumstances (such as a grossly inadequate price) can negate good faith status.

Void vs. Voidable Title (Land): A deed obtained by 'fraud in the execution' (trickery as to the instrument's character) is void. A deed obtained by 'fraud in the inducement' (misrepresentation about the underlying transaction) is merely voidable.

Negligence Exception to Void Deeds: While a void deed is generally a nullity and cannot pass title even to a BFP, an original owner who was negligent in signing the instrument may be estopped from asserting their title against a subsequent bona fide purchaser for value.
Bona Fide Purchaser (BFP): A BFP is a party who purchases property for valuable consideration without notice (actual, constructive, or inquiry) of any prior claim or competing interest.

cases.question: If a landowner is tricked into signing a deed that he believes is a lease, can he recover the land from an innocent third party who later bought it from the trickster?
cases.answer: The innocent purchasers win; although the deed was void due to fraud, the original owner's potential negligence in signing prevents him from invalidating the sale to a bona fide purchaser.
cases.why: This case establishes that an original owner's negligence can allow a void deed to become the root of good title for a BFP, prioritizing marketability over the original owner's absolute security.

cases.question: Can someone who buys a Rolex for a suspiciously low price from a person who obtained it with a bad check qualify as a 'good faith purchaser' and keep the watch from the original seller?
cases.answer: The original seller (Nowlin) wins because the buyer (Kotis) was not a good faith purchaser, as he willfully ignored suspicious facts like the very low price and the seller's evasiveness.
cases.why: This case defines the limits of the good faith purchaser doctrine for goods under the UCC, showing that the subjective standard of 'honesty in fact' does not protect a buyer who deliberately ignores red flags.

cases.question: When a property's value decreases after a land sale contract is signed but before the final payment and deed transfer, who is entitled to the settlement money for that loss—the seller holding legal title or the buyer making payments?
cases.answer: The buyer (Donohue) wins because the doctrine of equitable conversion makes the buyer the 'equitable owner' from the moment the contract is signed, entitling them to all benefits and risks of ownership.
cases.why: This case demonstrates how equitable conversion splits ownership upon contract signing, treating the buyer as the true owner for purposes of loss and gain, even before the formal transfer of legal title.

tensions: Protecting Original Owners vs. Promoting Marketability: The law constantly balances the security of the 'true' owner against the need for an efficient market where buyers can rely on the state of title. [[Hauck v. Crawford]] favors marketability by penalizing a negligent owner, while the baseline rule that a thief cannot pass title protects the original owner.

Subjective vs. Objective Standard for 'Good Faith': The UCC's 'honesty in fact' standard for good faith is subjective. However, as [[Kotis v. Nowlin Jewelry Inc.]] shows, courts may infer a lack of subjective honesty from objective facts, like a suspiciously low price, creating a tension between what a buyer actually believed and what a reasonable person would have believed.

Formal Title vs. Equitable Ownership: The doctrine of equitable conversion, seen in [[Wood v. Donohue]], creates a legal fiction where the person with formal legal title (the seller) is not the 'owner' for purposes of risk and benefit. This split between legal and equitable title can lead to outcomes that seem counterintuitive based on the paper title alone.
traps: Confusing Void and Voidable Title: Do not treat all fraudulent transfers identically. A thief gives VOID title, and a BFP always loses. A con artist who induces a voluntary transfer (e.g., with a bad check) gives VOIDABLE title, and a BFP can win. The outcome depends entirely on this distinction.

Forgetting the Negligence Exception for Void Deeds: In land transactions, simply concluding a deed is 'void' from fraud in the execution is not the end of the analysis. As in [[Hauck v. Crawford]], you must then ask if the original grantor was negligent, which could estop them from recovering from a BFP.

Misapplying Equitable Conversion: Equitable conversion is a default rule that shifts risk to the buyer upon contract signing. However, the parties can—and often do—contract around this default. Always check the facts for a contractual provision that re-allocates risk, such as an insurance clause.
title_transfer_land_transactions_good_fa.exam_tip: When analyzing a chain of title with a fraudulent transfer, follow a strict three-step process. 1) Classify the title held by the wrongdoer (void or voidable?). 2) Determine if the subsequent purchaser qualifies as a Bona Fide Purchaser (BFP) for value and without notice. 3) Apply the correct rule: a BFP loses to void title (unless the original owner was negligent, per [[Hauck]]) but wins against voidable title.

9. The Law of Neighbors.intro: This chapter, The Law of Neighbors, explores the legal frameworks governing relationships between adjacent landowners. It examines how an owner’s absolute rights can be limited by the rights of others. The units fit together as a spectrum of control: from private agreements creating rights of use (easements) and restrictions (covenants), to public regulation dictating land use for the collective good (zoning). This chapter directly addresses the course’s central question—when does the law side with the owner, and what beats ownership?—by demonstrating that neighbors’ reliance, private agreements that run with the land, and the state’s police power can all supersede an individual owner’s right to use or exclude others from their property.

easements.summary: An easement is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a specific purpose. It can be created expressly or, in certain situations, implied by law through prior use, necessity, prescription, or estoppel.

rules.rule: An easement by necessity requires: (1) common ownership of the two parcels prior to severance of the landlocked parcel, and (2) that the owner of the now landlocked parcel cannot access a public roadway from their own property. The necessity must exist at the time of severance.

An easement by implication arises from: (1) a separation of title; (2) a pre-existing use so obvious and continuous as to show it was meant to be permanent; and (3) the easement is necessary for the beneficial enjoyment of the land.
A prescriptive easement is acquired by use that is open, notorious, continuous, and adverse for an uninterrupted statutory period (e.g., five years in California).
A license to use land, normally revocable, becomes an irrevocable easement by estoppel if the licensee makes substantial expenditures in reasonable reliance on the license.

In the U.S., a landowner has no legal right to the free flow of light and air across adjoining land. A structure serving a useful purpose is not a nuisance even if it blocks light and air, regardless of spiteful motive.
cases: [[Fontainebleau Hotel Corp. v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five Inc.]]

rules.rule: A landowner who acquires a prescriptive easement is not required to compensate the burdened landowner for its fair market value.
A landowner cannot create their own necessity by conveying away their access to a public road and then claim an easement by necessity over their grantor's or a stranger's land.

cases.case: [[Fontainebleau Hotel Corp. v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five Inc.]]
cases.question: Does a landowner have a legal right to the free flow of light and air, such that they can stop a neighbor from building a structure that casts a shadow on their property?
cases.answer: Fontainebleau (the builder) won; American law rejects the English doctrine of 'ancient lights,' so there is no legal right to light and air absent an express agreement, statute, or easement.
cases.why: This case establishes the strong American rule prioritizing a landowner's right to build on their property over a neighbor's interest in light and air, a core principle of owner autonomy.

cases.question: Can a landowner revoke permission to use a road on their property after the user, with the owner's consent, spent money to improve the road and built a house relying on that access?
cases.answer: The Taylors (the users) won; a license becomes irrevocable by estoppel when the licensee makes substantial expenditures in reliance on it, creating an easement.
cases.why: This case provides the classic example of an easement by estoppel (or irrevocable license), where equity prevents a licensor from revoking permission after the licensee has relied on it to their detriment.

cases.question: Can a party who acquires a prescriptive easement be forced to pay the burdened landowner for the value of the easement or for the cost of removing an encroachment built to block it?
cases.answer: Warsaw (the easement user) won; a prescriptive easement is acquired without cost, and a landowner who willfully obstructs it during litigation may be ordered to remove the obstruction at their own expense.
cases.why: This case confirms that prescription, like adverse possession, results in a transfer of property rights without compensation and shows that a court may issue a mandatory injunction against a willful encroacher.

cases.question: Can landowners who landlocked their own parcels by selling off their road access claim an easement by necessity or implication over their neighbors' properties?
cases.answer: The neighbors won; an easement by necessity requires that the parcel was landlocked at the time of severance by the common grantor, and a party cannot create their own necessity.
cases.why: This case demonstrates the strict requirements for implied easements and the strong policy against creating 'hidden' burdens on land, especially when the hardship is self-inflicted.

tensions: Formalism vs. Equity: The strict, formal requirements for easements by necessity in [[Schwab v. Timmons]] contrast sharply with the flexible, equity-based creation of an irrevocable license in [[Holbrook v. Taylor]].

Owner Autonomy vs. Neighborly Fairness: [[Fontainebleau Hotel Corp. v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five Inc.]] champions a landowner's right to build whatever they want, while the dissent in [[Warsaw v. Chicago Metallic Ceilings Inc.]] argues for fairness by requiring a 'trespasser' to pay for the property right they acquire by prescription.

Economic Efficiency vs. Fairness: The majority in [[Warsaw v. Chicago Metallic Ceilings Inc.]] justifies no-compensation prescriptive easements as a way to stabilize long-term uses and reduce litigation, an efficiency argument. The dissent argues this is simply unjust enrichment and bad policy in a modern, planned society.
traps: Confusing Easement by Necessity and Implication: An easement by necessity requires that the parcel be strictly landlocked at the moment of severance. An easement by implication requires a pre-existing, apparent use and only reasonable necessity.

Forgetting the 'Self-Created Hardship' Rule: As seen in [[Schwab v. Timmons]], a plaintiff who sells off their own access to a road cannot then turn around and sue a neighbor for an easement by necessity. The necessity must arise from the severance by the common grantor.

Assuming All Non-Express Uses are Adverse: A prescriptive easement requires adverse use. If the owner gave permission, it's a license. However, as in [[Holbrook v. Taylor]], a license can become irrevocable through reliance and estoppel, creating a different kind of easement.

Applying the 'Ancient Lights' Doctrine: This English doctrine granting a right to light and air is a classic trap. [[Fontainebleau Hotel Corp. v. Forty-Five Twenty-Five Inc.]] makes clear it has been 'unanimously repudiated' in the United States.
easements.exam_tip: When you see a landlocked parcel, immediately analyze for an easement by necessity. Key questions: Was there a common owner? Was the parcel landlocked *at the moment of severance*? If the hardship was self-created, the claim fails ([[Schwab v. Timmons]]). If the use wasn't necessary but was long-standing and without permission, analyze for a prescriptive easement ([[Warsaw v. Chicago Metallic Ceilings Inc.]]).

covenants.summary: Covenants are promises regarding land use that can 'run with the land' to bind subsequent owners. For a covenant to run at law, it requires intent, privity, and that it 'touch and concern' the land; in equity, implied restrictions can be enforced if there is a common scheme and notice.

rules.rule: For a real covenant to run with the land, it must satisfy three requirements: (1) the parties intended it to run; (2) it 'touches and concerns' the land; and (3) there is 'privity of estate' between the parties.
cases: [[Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank]]

rules.rule: An affirmative covenant to pay money for the maintenance of common areas 'touches and concerns' the land because it substantially affects the legal rights of the landowners by burdening the land and providing a benefit to it.
cases: [[Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank]]

rules.rule: A property owners' association (HOA) can enforce a covenant even if it lacks strict privity of estate, as it is viewed as the agent or representative of the property owners who do have privity.
cases: [[Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank]]

rules.rule: A reciprocal negative easement (or implied equitable servitude) arises when a common owner sells lots with restrictions benefiting the retained land; the retained land then becomes mutually burdened, and the restriction binds subsequent purchasers with notice.
A purchaser has constructive notice of a reciprocal negative easement if the uniform residential character of the neighborhood would put a reasonable person on inquiry.
State court enforcement of a private, racially restrictive covenant constitutes state action and violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Fair Housing Act (FHA) does not apply to the selection of roommates within a shared living unit, as this implicates constitutional rights of privacy and intimate association.
cases: [[Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommate.com LLC]]

cases.question: Can a restrictive covenant for residential use only be enforced against a lot owner whose deed contains no such restriction, when most other lots in the subdivision are restricted?
cases.answer: The neighbors won; a 'reciprocal negative easement' was implied from the common development scheme, and the owner had constructive notice from the uniform residential character of the neighborhood.
cases.why: This is the key case for implied equitable servitudes, showing that restrictions can bind landowners even if not in their deed, as long as there was a common plan and notice.

cases.case: [[Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank]]
cases.question: Can an HOA enforce a covenant requiring a homeowner to pay fees for common area maintenance, even though the HOA doesn't own land and the covenant is affirmative?
cases.answer: The HOA won; the court looked past legal formalities to the substance, holding that the covenant 'touches and concerns' the land and that the HOA has standing to sue as the owners' agent.
cases.why: This case modernized the law of covenants, allowing for the enforcement of HOA fees by interpreting the 'touch and concern' and 'privity' requirements flexibly to suit modern subdivisions.

cases.question: Does judicial enforcement of a private agreement that restricts property ownership based on race violate the Fourteenth Amendment?
cases.answer: The Shelleys (the buyers) won; while private discrimination is not unconstitutional, court enforcement of that discrimination is 'state action' that violates the Equal Protection Clause.
cases.why: This landmark case establishes a major limit on the enforcement of private land use restrictions, demonstrating that constitutional principles can override private agreements when the state becomes the enforcer.

cases.case: [[Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommate.com LLC]]
cases.question: Does the Fair Housing Act, which prohibits discrimination in the rental of a 'dwelling,' apply to the selection of roommates within a shared apartment or house?
cases.answer: Roommate.com won; the FHA does not apply to roommate selection because regulating relationships inside the home would raise serious constitutional concerns regarding privacy and the right of intimate association.
cases.why: This case defines a crucial limit on anti-discrimination law, holding that the FHA stops at the 'front door' and does not regulate the choice of who to live with inside a shared home.

tensions: Formalism vs. Functionalism: [[Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank]] represents a shift from rigid, formal rules (e.g., strict privity) to a functional approach that recognizes the practical realities of modern housing developments and HOAs.

Freedom of Contract vs. Constitutional Rights: [[Shelley v. Kraemer]] shows that the freedom to create private land use agreements is not absolute; it is trumped by the Equal Protection Clause when state power is used to enforce discriminatory terms.

Anti-Discrimination Policy vs. Personal Liberty: [[Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommate.com LLC]] balances the public policy against housing discrimination with the constitutional right to privacy and association within one's home, ultimately prioritizing personal liberty in the context of roommate selection.
traps: Misapplying [[Shelley v. Kraemer]]: The trap is thinking it makes discriminatory covenants illegal. It does not. It only makes their *enforcement by a court* unconstitutional state action. Voluntary compliance is not prohibited by the holding.

Forgetting the Notice Requirement: For an implied servitude from a common scheme to be enforceable, the buyer must have had notice ([[Sanborn v. McLean]]). This can be actual notice, record notice (from other deeds in their chain of title), or inquiry notice (from the look of the neighborhood). No notice, no enforcement.

Overextending the [[Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommate.com LLC]] Holding: The ruling is narrow. It applies to sharing a living unit. It does *not* allow a landlord renting out a separate apartment or a small building to discriminate.

Ignoring the 'Touch and Concern' Test for Affirmative Covenants: Historically, affirmative covenants (promises to do something, like pay money) were disfavored. [[Neponsit Property Owners' Association v. Emigrant Industrial Savings Bank]] shows they can run with the land, but only if they are substantially related to the use and enjoyment of the property.
covenants.exam_tip: On an exam, if you see a restriction in a deed, run through the three `Neponsit` requirements for a covenant to run with the land: Intent, Touch & Concern, and Privity. If the restriction is *not* in the deed but the neighborhood looks uniform, switch to a `Sanborn` analysis for an implied reciprocal negative servitude and focus on whether there was a common plan and notice.

conservation_easements_zoning.summary: Zoning is the primary tool for public control of land use, allowing municipalities to regulate property for the general welfare. This power is broad but not unlimited; it must be rational, can be used to phase out nonconforming uses, and in some jurisdictions, must serve regional housing needs.

rules.rule: A comprehensive zoning ordinance is a constitutional exercise of the state's police power so long as its provisions are not clearly arbitrary and unreasonable, having no substantial relation to the public health, safety, morals, or general welfare.
cases: [[Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.]]

rules.rule: If the validity of a legislative classification for zoning purposes is 'fairly debatable,' the legislative judgment must be allowed to control.
cases: [[Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.]]

rules.rule: A municipality may require the termination of a pre-existing nonconforming use after a reasonable 'amortization' period, which allows the owner to recoup their investment.

The reasonableness of an amortization period for a nonconforming use is determined by balancing public benefit against private harm, considering factors like the owner's investment, the nature of the use, and the character of the neighborhood.
In New Jersey, a developing municipality's zoning power must be exercised for the 'general welfare' of the region, not just the municipality itself.
cases: [[Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel]]

rules.rule: A developing municipality has an affirmative obligation to use its zoning regulations to create a realistic opportunity for the development of its fair share of the present and prospective regional need for low- and moderate-income housing.
cases: [[Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel]]

rules.rule: A municipality may not enact 'exclusionary zoning'—such as minimum lot sizes, barring multi-family housing, or overzoning for industry—for the purpose of avoiding the fiscal burdens of lower-income residents.
cases: [[Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel]]

cases.case: [[Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.]]
cases.question: Is a comprehensive zoning ordinance that divides a village into districts for different uses (residential, commercial, industrial) and thereby reduces a property's value constitutional?
cases.answer: The Village of Euclid won; the Supreme Court held that comprehensive zoning is a legitimate exercise of the state's police power to protect public health, safety, and welfare.
cases.why: This landmark case established the constitutionality of zoning in the United States, providing the legal foundation for modern land use regulation by municipalities.

cases.question: Can a city force a business that pre-dates a zoning ordinance (a 'nonconforming use') to shut down after a specified grace period?
cases.answer: The City of Buffalo won; the court held that municipalities can require the termination of nonconforming uses after a 'reasonable amortization period' that allows the owner to recoup their investment.
cases.why: This case introduced and validated the concept of amortization, giving cities a tool to gradually eliminate nonconforming uses and achieve uniform zoning over time, rather than protecting such uses in perpetuity.

cases.case: [[Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel]]
cases.question: Can a developing municipality use its zoning power to enact regulations (like large lot sizes and bans on apartments) that make it impossible for low- and moderate-income people to live there?
cases.answer: The NAACP won; the New Jersey Supreme Court held that a developing municipality's zoning must promote the 'general welfare' of the entire region, which includes providing a realistic opportunity for its 'fair share' of regional low- and moderate-income housing.
cases.why: This case created the 'Mount Laurel Doctrine,' a powerful check on exclusionary ('NIMBY') zoning that requires municipalities to consider regional housing needs and affirmatively plan for affordable housing.

tensions: Individual Property Rights vs. Collective Good: [[Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.]] squarely addresses this tension, finding that the community's interest in an orderly, safe environment can justify significant restrictions on an individual's property rights and value.

Vested Rights vs. Community Evolution: [[Harbison v. City of Buffalo]] pits the right of an owner to continue a long-standing, lawful use against a community's desire to evolve and improve. The 'amortization' concept is the compromise, allowing change while attempting to be fair to the owner.

Local Control vs. Regional Responsibility: [[Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel]] directly challenges the idea of pure localism in zoning, holding that a town's 'general welfare' is tied to the welfare of the surrounding region, especially regarding the fundamental need for housing.
traps: Assuming Zoning is a Taking: A common mistake is to think that any zoning ordinance that reduces property value is an unconstitutional taking requiring compensation. [[Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.]] establishes that zoning is a valid exercise of police power, and diminution in value alone does not make it a taking.

Believing Nonconforming Uses are Perpetual: Before [[Harbison v. City of Buffalo]], the right to a nonconforming use was often seen as a protected, vested right. The trap is to forget that many jurisdictions now allow municipalities to eliminate these uses over time through reasonable amortization.

Limiting 'General Welfare' to Town Borders: The traditional view of zoning is purely local. The trap is to ignore the revolutionary impact of [[Southern Burlington County NAACP v. Township of Mount Laurel]], which expands the concept of 'general welfare' to include regional needs, at least in New Jersey and states that follow its logic.

Ignoring the 'Fairly Debatable' Standard: When challenging a zoning ordinance, it's not enough to show a better way to zone the property. Under the deferential standard from [[Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.]], if the municipality's decision is 'fairly debatable,' the court will not interfere.
conservation_easements_zoning.exam_tip: If a fact pattern involves a zoning ordinance, first check if it's facially valid under the rational basis test from `Euclid`. If the ordinance affects a pre-existing use, analyze the issue as a nonconforming use and discuss the reasonableness of any amortization period per `Harbison`. If the ordinance appears to exclude types of housing or people, apply the `Mount Laurel` framework to analyze whether the town is failing its 'fair share' obligation to the region.

10. Government Forbearance and Takings.intro: This chapter explores the constitutional limits on the government's power to interfere with private property. The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause and the Constitution's Contract Clause act as shields for the owner against the state's immense power. The units trace the contours of this conflict. First, we see how the Contract Clause limits the government's ability to walk back its own promises. Next, we examine the government's explicit power to take property via eminent domain, focusing on the requirements of 'public use' and 'just compensation.' Finally, we analyze when a government regulation becomes so burdensome it functions as a 'taking,' and whether a court itself can take property by redefining legal rights. This chapter directly addresses the course's central question: what can defeat ownership? The answer is often the government, but only within these constitutional boundaries.

contract_clause_government_forbearance.summary: This unit examines how the Contract Clause limits a state's power to pass laws that impair its own prior agreements, especially corporate charters and public grants.

rules.rule: Public grants from the government to private parties are to be construed strictly against the grantee and in favor of the public.
An exclusive privilege or a covenant not to authorize competition will not be implied in a public grant; it must be explicitly stated.
The government's sovereign power to promote public welfare and provide new infrastructure is not presumed to be surrendered by implication in a grant.
A state law may be retrospective in its operation and divest vested rights without violating the U.S. Constitution, so long as it does not impair the obligation of a contract.

cases.question: Can a state legislature authorize a new, competing bridge that devalues an existing chartered bridge, if the original charter did not explicitly grant an exclusive right?
cases.answer: Warren Bridge (the new bridge) wins; a state can authorize competition because public grants are construed strictly, and an exclusive right will not be implied.
cases.why: This case establishes the rule of strict construction for public grants, prioritizing the state's power to promote public welfare and technological progress over protecting private monopolies based on implied contract rights.

tensions: The tension between protecting the stability of private investments made in reliance on government grants and allowing the government the flexibility to promote public welfare, new technology, and economic development.

The conflict between the majority's strict construction of public grants and Justice Story's dissent, which argued that common law at the time implied exclusivity to protect the franchise's value, reflecting a broader debate about how to interpret government contracts.
traps: Confusing the Contract Clause with the Takings Clause. [[Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge]] was decided under the Contract Clause: the charter contained no promise of exclusivity, so authorizing a competing bridge impaired no contract. Whether a government act is a taking is a separate question with its own tests.

Assuming any government action that reduces a business's value is a constitutional violation. [[Charles River Bridge]] shows that lawful competition, even when enabled by the government, is not a breach of contract unless an explicit promise of exclusivity was made.
contract_clause_government_forbearance.exam_tip: When a fact pattern involves a government grant followed by a new law that harms the grantee's business, first check the original grant for an explicit promise of exclusivity. If there isn't one, apply the [[Charles River Bridge]] rule: strict construction against the grantee, no implied rights, and deference to the state's promotion of public welfare.

takings_eminent_domain_just_compensation.summary: This unit covers the government's power of eminent domain—the power to physically take private property for 'public use' upon payment of 'just compensation,' as required by the Fifth Amendment.

rules.rule: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause permits the government to take private property for 'public use' so long as it provides 'just compensation.'
The 'public use' requirement is broadly interpreted to be synonymous with 'public purpose,' and courts afford legislatures broad deference in determining what constitutes a public purpose.
Economic development can qualify as a 'public use,' even when it involves transferring property to a private entity, if it is part of a carefully considered, comprehensive development plan.
A taking for the mere pretext of a public purpose, when its actual purpose is to bestow a private benefit, is unconstitutional.
'Just compensation' is the full and perfect equivalent in money for the property taken, generally measured by its fair market value.

Just compensation should not include any increase in value that is attributable to the very project for which the government is taking the land, if the land was probably within the scope of the project from the time the government committed to it.

cases.question: When the government condemns land, must 'just compensation' include any increase in the land's market value that resulted from the government's own project?
cases.answer: The United States wins; just compensation excludes any 'project-enhanced value' if the property was likely within the project's scope from the beginning.
cases.why: This case establishes a key limit on 'just compensation,' ensuring the government does not have to pay for value it created and preventing owners from getting a windfall from the public project.

cases.question: Can a city take non-blighted private property and transfer it to a private developer for the purpose of economic development?
cases.answer: The City of New London wins; the Court held that a carefully planned economic development project qualifies as a 'public use' under the Fifth Amendment.
cases.why: This case affirmed a very broad, deferential standard for 'public use,' equating it with 'public purpose' and establishing that economic development is a valid justification for eminent domain, even if it benefits private parties.

tensions: The conflict between the [[Kelo]] majority's broad, deferential interpretation of 'public use' as 'public purpose' and the dissents' call for a narrower interpretation that would require literal public use or the correction of a public harm.

The definition of 'just compensation' focuses on objective fair market value ([[United States v. Miller]]), which may fail to compensate owners for subjective value, community ties, or the indignity of a forced sale.
traps: Forgetting the 'scope of the project' rule from [[United States v. Miller]]. If a property's value increases because of a new government project, and the government later expands the project to condemn that property, the owner is not entitled to the value increase caused by the project.

Assuming a taking is invalid just because property is transferred from one private owner to another. After [[Kelo]], the key question is whether the transfer serves a legitimate public purpose (like economic revitalization) as part of a comprehensive plan, not just who ends up with the land.
takings_eminent_domain_just_compensation.exam_tip: When analyzing an eminent domain problem, address two distinct questions: (1) Is it for a 'public use'? Apply the deferential [[Kelo]] standard unless the facts strongly suggest a pretext for pure private benefit. (2) Is the compensation 'just'? Start with fair market value, then subtract any project-enhanced value under the [[Miller]] rule.

takings_regulatory_judicial.summary: This unit addresses when a government regulation becomes so burdensome that it is a 'taking' requiring compensation, and explores the newer concept of a 'judicial taking,' where a court decision itself might take property.

rules.rule: While property may be regulated, if a regulation 'goes too far,' it will be recognized as a taking requiring compensation under the Fifth Amendment.
A regulation that deprives land of all economically beneficial or productive use is a categorical taking.
Exception: A total deprivation of economic use is not a taking if the proscribed use was already prohibited by background principles of the state's law of property and nuisance.

For regulations that are not categorical takings, courts apply an ad hoc balancing test considering: (1) the economic impact, (2) interference with distinct investment-backed expectations, and (3) the character of the governmental action.
cases: [[Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City]]

rules.rule: In a takings analysis, the court looks at the parcel as a whole, rather than dividing it into discrete segments (e.g., air rights, mineral rights) to see if one segment was totally taken.
cases: [[Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City]]

rules.rule: Judicial takings (unsettled): a four-Justice plurality in [[Stop the Beach Renourishment Inc. v. Florida Department of Environmental Protection]] would hold that a court decision is a taking if it declares that an established property right no longer exists; the other Justices did not reach or rejected that view.

cases.question: Can a state law prohibit coal mining that causes subsidence, even when the company expressly reserved the right to do so, without paying compensation?
cases.answer: Pennsylvania Coal Co. wins; the law went 'too far' by making the reserved mining rights commercially worthless, which was functionally equivalent to a taking.
cases.why: This case established the foundational concept of a 'regulatory taking,' where a government regulation, not just a physical seizure, can be a Fifth Amendment taking if it is too severe.

cases.case: [[Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City]]
cases.question: Does a historic landmark law that prevents the owner of Grand Central Terminal from building an office tower above it constitute a taking?
cases.answer: New York City wins; the law was not a taking because it did not interfere with the owner's primary investment-backed expectations and allowed for a reasonable return on the property as a whole.
cases.why: This case established the flexible, multi-factor balancing test for most regulatory takings claims and articulated the 'parcel as a whole' rule.

cases.question: Is a state regulation that prohibits all construction on a property, rendering it economically valueless, a taking?
cases.answer: Lucas wins; a regulation that deprives a property of all economically beneficial use is a categorical taking unless the prohibited use was already barred by state nuisance or property law.
cases.why: This case created a per se rule for 'total takings,' carving out a category of regulations that are compensable without the ad hoc balancing of [[Penn Central]].

cases.case: [[Stop the Beach Renourishment Inc. v. Florida Department of Environmental Protection]]
cases.question: Can a state supreme court decision itself be a taking, and did the Florida court's ruling on beach ownership rights constitute one?
cases.answer: Florida won, unanimously: the Florida Supreme Court's decision did not eliminate any established property right. A four-Justice plurality would recognize judicial takings; the rest of the Court declined to decide that question.
cases.why: A plurality proposed extending takings analysis to court decisions; the Court did not adopt it, so judicial takings remain an open question.

tensions: The conflict between having clear, categorical rules ([[Lucas]]) versus flexible, ad hoc standards ([[Penn Central]]) for determining when a regulation becomes a taking.

The 'denominator problem': When measuring economic impact, should the court look at the value lost from the regulated portion (e.g., the coal in [[Pennsylvania Coal]]) or the value of the entire property parcel ([[Penn Central]])?

The unsettled nature of 'judicial takings' after [[Stop the Beach Renourishment]]. The plurality recognized the doctrine under the Takings Clause, but concurrences suggested the Due Process Clause is a better fit, leaving the doctrine's future uncertain.
traps: Applying the [[Lucas]] 'total wipeout' rule when there is only a partial loss of value. If the property retains any economically beneficial use, you must use the [[Penn Central]] balancing test, not the [[Lucas]] categorical rule.
Forgetting the 'background principles' exception in [[Lucas]]. Even if a regulation causes a total wipeout, it's not a taking if the owner's proposed use was already illegal under state nuisance law.

Declaring a judicial taking too quickly. Only a four-Justice plurality in [[Stop the Beach Renourishment Inc. v. Florida Department of Environmental Protection]] recognized judicial takings, and even on its view a decision is a taking only if it eliminates a clearly established property right; clarifying unsettled law or ordinary common-law development is not.
takings_regulatory_judicial.exam_tip: For a regulatory taking, use this flowchart: 1) Is it a physical invasion? If yes, it's a taking. 2) Does it deprive the property of ALL economically beneficial use? If yes, it's a [[Lucas]] categorical taking (but check the 'background principles' exception). 3) If no to both, it's a partial taking, so you must apply the [[Penn Central]] three-factor balancing test.
